profileDesc.creation:
Initially created: 2025-12-06T13:38:02.584+09:00 by chris Translate the following text from Classical Chinese into English.
Requirements: 1. The text contains page numbers in square brackets, such as [01], [02], etc. - These must be passed through unchanged. - Each page number must appear in exactly the same position in the translation as in the source. - The number of page markers in the output must match the input exactly.
2. Personal names, place names, titles, and other proper nouns should be rendered in Hànyǔ Pīnyīn with tone marks.
3. Do NOT transcribe the full Classical Chinese text into Pinyin.
4. Do NOT include explanatory notes, annotations, or commentary — output only the English translation.
5. The target language is English.

p.seg: Sīmǎ Guāng
compiled by imperial command
Later Student Tiāntāi
Sui Annals, Part One
Beginning in the year Túyī Zuò'è (Jǐyǒu),
ending in the year Chóngguāng Dàyuānxiàn (Xīnhài),
covering three years in total.
Sui
was originally the state of Suí from the Spring and Autumn period.
It was destroyed by the state of Chǔ,
and made into a county.
During the Qín and Hàn dynasties, it belonged to Nányáng Commandery.
During the Jìn dynasty, it belonged to Yìyáng Commandery.
Later, a separate Suí Commandery was established.
During the Liáng dynasty, it was called Suí Prefecture.
It later came under the control of Western Wèi.
Yáng Zhōng followed Zhōu Tàizǔ
and was enfeoffed as Duke of Suí for his merits.
His son Jiān inherited the title.
He received the abdication of the Zhōu dynasty,
and thus took Suí as the name of his state.
Furthermore, because the Zhōu and Qí dynasties were restless and unsettled,
he removed
"辶 + 隋"
and made it
because "辶 + 隋" signifies fleeing.
pronounced chuò.
Emperor Gāozǔ, the Civil Emperor, First Part, First Section
His personal name was Jiān,
surname Yáng.
The Book of Suí states: He was a native of Huàyīn in Hóngnóng Commandery.
Yáng Xuàn, the eighth-generation descendant of Hàn Grand Commandant Yáng Zhèn,
fathered Yáng Yuánshòu.
During Later Wèi, Yuánshòu served as Sima of Wǔchuān Garrison.
His descendants thus settled there.
Yáng Zhōng was the great-great-grandson of Yuánshòu.
He followed Zhōu Tàizǔ in raising an army west of the passes.
He fathered the Emperor.
From the thirteenth year of Chén Xuāndì's Tàijiàn era to the ninth year of the Kāihuáng era,
Sui had held the northwest for eight years.
Because the Comprehensive Mirror uses this ninth year as the beginning of Sui's reign period in its annals,
it is titled "First Part, First Section."
The ninth year of Kāihuáng
(Jǐyǒu, 589)
The Emperor received the abdication of the Zhōu dynasty in the thirteenth year of Chén Gāozōng's Tàijiàn era.
By this year, he had pacified Chén,
unifying all under heaven.
For recording events, the Comprehensive Mirror
uses the Kāihuáng reign period for dating.
1 Spring,
first month,
the first day being Yǐchǒu.
The Lord of Chén held court and assembled his ministers.
A great fog filled the four directions,
entering people's noses,
all felt acrid and sour.
The Lord of Chén fell into a deep sleep,
and did not wake until the bū hour.
The bū hour is when the sun reaches the shēn position.
Bū,
pronounced bēn mó fān.
On this day,
Hèruò Bì led troops from Guǎnglíng across the river.
Previously, Bì had used old horses to purchase many Chén ships and hide them.
He bought fifty or sixty worn-out ships
and placed them in inland waterways.
The Chén people spied on this,
and thought the interior country had no ships.
Bì also requested that the river defense troops, during each shift change,
must assemble at Guǎnglíng.
Thus, they displayed numerous banners and flags,
with tents covering the fields.
The Chén people thought the Sui troops had arrived in great force,
and urgently dispatched troops for defense.
Once they learned it was just a shift change for the defense troops,
their forces dispersed again.
Later, this became routine,
and they no longer made defensive preparations.
He also had troops hunt along the river from time to time,
with men and horses creating clamor.
Therefore, when Bì crossed the river,
the Chén people did not notice.
Hán Qínhǔ led five hundred men from Héngjiāng, crossing at night to Cǎishí.
Héngjiāng Pǔ
is within the boundaries of Hé Prefecture.
Cǎishí Jī
is located thirty lǐ north of present-day Tàipíng Prefecture, at the ferry crossing on the opposite bank.
Led,
pronounced jí liàng fān;
similarly for "led troops" below.
Thus, he captured it.
The events at Shāwǔkǒu in the twelfth month of the Jiǎxū year of Déyòu were similar to this.
The Sui Annals state: Liùhé County of Jiāngdū Commandery,
formerly called Wèishì,
had Qín Commandery established there.
Later Qí established Qín Prefecture there.
Later Zhōu changed the prefecture name to Fāng Prefecture,
and changed the commandery name to Liùhé.
Early in the Kāihuáng era,
the commandery was abolished.
In the fourth year,
Wèishì was renamed Liùhé.
Zhāng Shùnmín said: Táoyè Mountain
is the location of present-day Guābù Town.
Commander,
read as shuài.
Bǐngyín,
the garrison commander of Cǎishí, Xú Zǐjiàn, galloped to report the emergency.
Dīngmǎo,
he summoned the dukes and ministers to discuss military affairs.
Wùchén,
the Lord of Chén issued an edict stating:
"The dogs and sheep run rampant,
invading and encroaching upon the suburban borders.
Wasps and scorpions are poisonous,
they should be swept away and pacified in due time.
I shall personally lead the six armies,
to cleanse the eight directions,
and both inside and outside, a state of alert shall be enforced."
He appointed General of Agile Cavalry Xiāo Móhē, General of the Guard of the Army Fán Yì, and Central Army Commander Lǚ Guǎngdá as Commanders-in-Chief.
Minister of Works Sima Xiāonán and Xiāng Prefecture Governor Shī Wénqìng were appointed as Grand Army Supervisors.
Last winter,
the Lord of Chén promoted Shī Wénqìng to oversee Xiāng Prefecture,
but before he could reach his post, the Sui troops crossed the river.
Nán,
pronounced nǎi dàn fān.
Supervisor,
pronounced gōng xián fān.
Chén's Nányù Prefecture was administered from Xuānchéng,
but at that time, its headquarters was moved to Gūshú.
Báixià City combined with Báishí Fortress.
In the Wǔdé era of Táng, Jiāngníng County was moved here,
and named Báixià County.
Commander,
read as shuài.
He re-established reward standards,
and ordered monks, nuns, and Taoist priests
all to perform labor service.
Gēngwǔ,
Hèruò Bì attacked and captured Jīngkǒu,
capturing Nánxú Prefecture Governor Huáng Kè.
Nánxú Prefecture was administered from Jīngkǒu.
Not the slightest harm was done.
There was a soldier who bought wine from the common people,
Bì immediately beheaded him.
Over six thousand people were captured.
Bì released them all,
provided them with provisions, consoled them, and sent them off,
giving them proclamations
to disseminate and announce along various routes.
Thus, wherever they went, submission followed like the wind.
Fán Měng was in Jiànkāng.
His son Fán Xún acted as administrator of Nányù Prefecture affairs.
Xīnwèi,
Hán Qínhǔ advanced and attacked Gūshú.
In half a day,
he captured it,
and seized Xún and his family.
Present-day Tàipíng Prefecture Dāngtú County has Gūshú Stream two lǐ to the south,
which flows west into the great river.
It seems the old town derived its name from this.
He returned south of the river.
The elders had long heard of Qínhǔ's prestige and trustworthiness.
Those coming to pay respects at the army gate did not cease day or night.
Lǚ Guǎngdá's son Lǚ Shìzhēn was in Xīncài.
Together with his younger brother Shìxióng and their troops, they surrendered to Qínhǔ.
During the rebellion of Hóu Jǐng,
Lǚ Xīdá gathered fellow villagers to defend Xīncài.
Thus, the Lǚ clan served Chén for generations.
For notes on Xīncài, see the first year of Liáng Shìzǔ's Chéngshèng era in scroll 154.
Surrendered,
pronounced hù jiāng fān.
Guǎngdá was then stationed at Jiànkāng.
He impeached himself,
and went to the Court of Justice to request punishment.
The Lord of Chén consoled him,
bestowed additional gold upon him,
and sent him back to camp.
Fán Měng and Left Guard General Jiǎng Yuánxùn commanded eighty "Green Dragon" ships patrolling at Báixià,
to defend against the troops from Liùhé.
The Lord of Chén, because Měng's wife and children were in the Sui army,
feared he might have different intentions,
wanted to have General-in-Chief of the Eastern Garrison Rèn Zhōng replace him,
and ordered Xiāo Móhē to gently persuade Měng.
Měng was displeased.
The Lord of Chén, finding it difficult to hurt his feelings, stopped.
Difficult,
read according to its usual pronunciation,
meaning hard to do.
Then Hèruò Bì advanced from the northern route,
and Hán Qínhǔ advanced from the southern route simultaneously.
Jīngkǒu is north of Jiànkāng,
and Gūshú is south of Jiànkāng.
The enemy fled upon hearing the news;
Bì divided his troops and cut off the strategic point of Qū’ē and entered.
Qū’ē,
originally Yúnyáng,
during the Qin dynasty,
it was said that the land had imperial aura.
First Emperor dug a pit to break its force,
making the direct path bend,
hence renamed Qū’ē.
It is located between Wǔjìn and Dāntú counties.
Bì divided his troops to sever the strategic point,
fearing that the armies from Sān Wú would enter to rescue Jiànkāng,
reinforcing from the rear.
"Sever,"
pronounced as "short."
Xiāo Móhē stationed at Lèyóu Garden,
Fán Yì stationed at Qíshé Temple,
Lǔ Guǎngdá stationed at Bái Tǔ Gāng,
Zhōngwǔ General Kǒng Fàn stationed at Bǎotián Temple,
Zhōngwǔ General,
established by Liáng,
placed as rank nineteen;
Chén proposed fourth rank for officials,
salary equating two thousand dàn of grain,
ranked below Sìpíng General.
On the day Jǐmǎo,
Rèn Zhōng entered from Wúxīng,
having been sent to govern Wúxīng the previous year.
Jìn Emperor Xiàowǔ built the Zhūquè Gate,
with two bronze sparrows atop,
directly before the grand bridge,
called the Zhūquè Bridge.
On the day Xīnwèi,
Hèruò Bì advanced and took Zhōngshān,
located eighteen lǐ northeast of today's Shàngyuán county.
Geographical records: formerly called Jīnlíng Mountain,
the county name derives from this.
Also known as Jiǎngshān,
during the end of the Han, Mòlíng magistrate Jiǎng Zǐwén died here fighting bandits,
the Sūn clan ruled Mòlíng,
to honor their ancestor's name Zhōng,
it was renamed Jiǎngshān.
Jìn Prince Wáng Guǎng sent Commander Dù Yàn to join forces with Hán Qínhǔ,
twenty thousand infantry and cavalry camped at Xīnlín.
Xīnlín Pǔ,
twenty lǐ from today's Jiànkāng city,
west of Báilù Isle.
Defeated General Jì Tián of Chén at Qíkǒu,
where the Qí River enters the Yangtze.
General,
pronounces as "liàng,"
similarly below.
Tián,
pronounces as "tā diàn,"
also "zhèn."
Surrender followed one after another.
Jìn Prince Wáng Guǎng reported the situation,
Emperor was delighted,
hosting a banquet and rewarding officials.
At the time, Jiànkāng still had over a hundred thousand armored soldiers,
but Emperor Chén was naturally timid,
neglecting the military,
only crying day and night,
managing palace affairs,
all entrusted to Shī Wénqìng.
Knowing the generals despised him,
fearing they might achieve success,
he announced:
"This cohort is resentful,
not complying with commands,
under such urgency,
how can we trust them!"
Hence, whenever the generals made requests,
none were executed.
When Hèruò Bì attacked Jīngkǒu,
Xiāo Móhē sought permission to lead troops to counterattack,
but Emperor Chén did not allow it.
When Bì reached Zhōngshān,
Móhē again said:
"Bì's army is deep within and unsupported,
the fortifications are not strong,
sending troops for a surprise attack,
would guarantee victory."
Again, it was not permitted.
Emperor Chén summoned Móhē and Rèn Zhōng to the inner palace to discuss military matters,
Zhōng said:
"Military strategy values quick action for the attacker,
but caution for the defender.
Now, the nation has ample troops and supplies,
we should securely defend the capital,
build barricades along the Huái River,
even if northern troops come,
do not engage them;
divide forces to block the Yangtze route,
preventing their communication.
Provide me with ten thousand elite soldiers,
and three hundred golden-winged ships,
I will descend the Yangtze to capture Liùhé;
their grand army would think those who crossed the river are captured,
naturally lowering morale.
The people south of the Huái are familiar with me,
upon hearing my arrival,
they will surely follow me.
Shīgǔ said: "Follow as shadows follow form."
Sever their retreat path,
their armies will disband without a fight.
Xuzhou,
the route of Péng and Biàn.”
Defend,
pronounces as "fú yòu."
Sever,
pronounces as "dīng guǎn."
The Jiangzhou troops like Zhōu Luóhóu will surely flow to aid.
Zhōu Luóhóu, at the time commanding the naval forces,
stationed at Yǐnghàn.
Emperor Chén could not follow this.
The following day,
suddenly declared:
"Lingering without resolution,
causes irritation,
call Xiāo Láng to strike once!"
Rèn Zhōng knelt, pleading against battle.
Kǒng Fàn also reported:
"Request to make a decisive move,
to engrave official achievements on Yànrán.”
Kǒng Fàn, referencing Dòu Xiàn's victory over the Xiongnu,
arrogantly compared himself.
His flattery led to national and family ruin.
"For,"
pronounces as "yú wěi."
Below the same.
Said to Móhē:
"You can decide for me!"
Móhē said:
"In past campaigns,
I acted for the nation and myself;
today's matters involve my family too."
Emperor Chén issued abundant gold and silk to the troops as rewards.
"Allocate,"
giving,
distributing.
On the day Jiǎshēn,
ordered Lǔ Guǎngdá to form ranks at Bái Tǔ Gāng,
positioned south of the armies,
followed by Rèn Zhōng,
then Fán Yì and Kǒng Fàn,
Xiāo Móhē's troops were at the farthest north.
The positions stretched twenty lǐ from south to north,
unaware of front or rear movements.
Hèruò Bì led light cavalry up the mountain,
saw the army,
hurried down,
assembling his force of eight thousand armored soldiers under the command of Subcommanders Yáng Yá, Yuán Míng, and others
into formation waiting.
Emperor Chén was involved with Xiāo Móhē's wife,
thus Móhē initially lacked the will to fight;
only Lǔ Guǎngdá and his followers fought fiercely,
engaging directly with Bì.
The Suí army retreated several times,
suffering two hundred seventy-three deaths under Bì's command;
Bì used smoke to conceal himself,
distressed then rallied.
Chén soldiers took heads as trophies,
offering them to Emperor Chén for rewards,
Bì, aware of their arrogance and laziness,
redirected his troops towards Kǒng Fàn;
Fàn's forces briefly engaged then fled,
the Chén troops looked back,
causing the cavalry to collapse and scatter,
unable to be stopped, resulting in five thousand deaths.
Yuán Míng captured Xiāo Móhē,
delivering him to Bì,
Bì ordered his execution,
yet Móhē remained composed;
Bì then released and treated him with respect.
Rén Zhōng galloped into the palace,
reported the defeat to the Chén sovereign,
and said:
"Your Majesty should stay well.
'Hǎo'
means 'fitting';
'zhù',
means 'to stop'.
People in the south still say this today.
The Chén sovereign gave him two bundles of gold,
ordering him to recruit men to go out and fight.
Rén Zhōng said:
"Your Majesty should only prepare boats and oars,
and join the armies upstream."
This meant going to join Zhōu Luóhóu and others.
The Chén sovereign believed him,
ordered Rén Zhōng to go out and make arrangements,
and commanded the palace ladies to dress and pack, waiting for him,
wondering why he was gone for so long.
At that time, Hán Qínhǔ was advancing his army from Xīnlín,
and Rén Zhōng had already led several horsemen to surrender and welcome him at Shízǐgāng.
The commanding general Cài Zhēng was guarding the Zhūquè Bridge,
and upon hearing that Hán Qínhǔ was about to arrive,
his troops, terrified, scattered.
Rén Zhōng led Hán Qínhǔ's army straight into the Zhūquè Gate.
The Chén troops wanted to fight,
but Rén Zhōng waved them off, saying:
"Even an old man like me has surrendered,
what are you soldiers doing!"
"Jūn"
is sometimes written as
"jūn".
Thereupon, all civil and military officials within the city fled,
leaving only the Minister of Works Yuán Xiàn in the palace hall,
and a few others, including the Chief Minister Jiāng Zǒng, in the government offices.
The Chén sovereign said to Yuán Xiàn:
"I have never treated you better than others,
and today I am filled with nothing but regret.
This is like Liú Shàn's relationship with Xì Zhèng.
It also marks the end of the cultured elite of Jiāngdōng."
The Chén sovereign, panicked,
was about to hide,
but Yuán Xiàn sternly said:
"When the northern troops enter,
they will certainly not commit any offenses.
With matters as grave as this,
where does Your Majesty intend to go?
I wish for Your Majesty to straighten your robes and crown,
ascend the main hall,
and follow the precedent of Emperor Wǔ of Liáng receiving Hóu Jǐng."
This event is recorded in the 162nd scroll, in the third year of the Tàiqīng era of Emperor Wǔ of Liáng.
The sovereign pushed him aside and hurried away,
saying:
"Under the edge of blades,
one cannot confront them directly.
I have my own plan!"
He went out from the rear hall, Jǐngyáng Hall, with over ten palace ladies,
intending to throw himself into a well.
Yuán Xiàn pleaded bitterly, but he would not listen;
the palace attendant Xiàhóu Gōngyùn blocked the well with his body,
and the Chén sovereign struggled with him.
After a long time,
he finally managed to get in.
Soon after, soldiers looked into the well,
called out,
but received no response.
As they were about to throw stones down,
they heard a cry;
they pulled him up with a rope,
surprised by how heavy he was.
When he emerged,
it turned out he was tied together with Guìpín Zhāng and Guìpín Kǒng.
Zhù Mù said: The Jǐngyáng Well is in Fǎbǎo Temple.
Some say
there is a small pond beneath the Báilián Pavilion,
about ten feet square.
Others say
it is beside the Lǎnhuī Pavilion in Bǎoníng Temple.
An old legend says: The well's rim has a stone vein;
if you wipe it with silk,
it leaves a rouge mark.
Hence it is also called the Rouge Well,
or the Well of Humiliation.
Under the Liáng system: There were Palace Attendants and Acting Attendants.
Under the Chén system: Palace Attendants held the third-rank honorary position,
and Acting Attendants held the third-rank meritorious position,
outside the nine-rank system.
The Rear Hall Attendant
was likely a Palace Attendant stationed at the rear hall.
The Crown Prince, Shēn, aged fifteen,
sat with his chamber doors closed,
with the attendant Kǒng Bóyú serving by his side.
This was a Crown Prince's Attendant.
Under the Liáng system: There were four Palace Secretaries for the Crown Prince,
responsible for the regulations of his quarters;
and sixteen Attendants,
responsible for documentation.
Palace Secretaries were in the eighth class,
Attendants in the third class.
Under the Chén system: Palace Secretaries had a salary of six hundred shi,
and Attendants were the same.
Shēn sat calmly,
and consoled them, saying:
"The army is on the march,
there is no need for you to labor!"
The soldiers all paid their respects to him.
At that time, there were over a hundred members of the Chén imperial clan, princes, and marquises in Jiànkāng.
Fearing they might cause trouble,
the Chén sovereign summoned them all,
ordered them to gather in the court hall,
and put them under the overall command of the Prince of Yùzhāng, Shūyīng,
while secretly making preparations against them.
When the palace city fell,
they all surrendered together.
Hèruò Bì, riding the momentum of victory, reached Lèyóu Gardens.
Lǔ Guǎngdá was still leading his remaining troops in bitter, unceasing combat,
killing and capturing several hundred men.
As dusk fell,
he finally removed his armor,
faced the palace, bowed twice, and wept bitterly,
saying to his men:
"I could not save the state with my own body,
my crime is profound!"
His soldiers all wept and sighed,
and then he was captured.
The guards at all the gates fled.
That night, Hèruò Bì burned the Běiyè Gate and entered.
Hearing that Hán Qínhǔ had already captured Chén Shúbǎo,
he called for him to be brought to see him.
Shúbǎo, terrified,
sweat pouring down and legs trembling,
bowed twice to Bì.
Bì said to him:
"The ruler of a small state bowing to a minister of a great state
is in accordance with ritual.
When you enter the court, you will not lose your status as the Marquis of Guīmìng.
There is no need for fear."
Later, ashamed that his achievement came after Hán Qínhǔ's,
he quarreled with Qínhǔ,
drew his blade and went out;
he wanted to order Cài Zhēng to write a surrender note for Shúbǎo,
and command him to ride a mule cart to come to him,
but this did not come to pass.
Bì placed Shúbǎo in Déjiào Hall,
under military guard.
Gāo Jiǒng entered Jiànkāng first.
Jiǒng's son, Déhóng, was the records officer for Prince Guǎng of Jìn.
Guǎng sent Déhóng galloping to where Jiǒng was,
ordering him to spare Zhāng Lìhuá.
Jiǒng said:
"In ancient times, Tàigōng covered his face to execute Dájǐ.
Dájǐ
was a beautiful woman of the Yǒusū clan,
favored by King Zhòu of Shāng.
When King Wǔ defeated the Yīn,
he killed Zhòu,
and also executed Dájǐ.
'Dá',
should be pronounced 'gē'.
'Jǐ',
is pronounced 'jǐ'."
He then beheaded her at Qīngxī.
Déhóng returned to report,
and Guǎng's face changed color as he said:
"As the ancients said,
'There is no kindness that goes unrequited.'"
These are words from the poem 'Yì' in the Dàyǎ section of the Shījīng.
From then on, he bore a grudge against Jiǒng.
If Gāo Jiǒng had spared Lìhuá and Guǎng had taken her in,
Emperor Wén would certainly have been angry.
How then could he have later succeeded in his plot to seize the heir position?
He truly should have been grateful to him for this,
why bear a grudge instead!
The history is laying the groundwork for Guǎng's later killing of Jiǒng.
On the bǐngxū day,
Prince Guǎng of Jìn entered Jiànkāng.
Because Shī Wénqìng, having received responsibility, was disloyal,
twisting facts with flattery and deceit to blind and deafen his ruler,
and Shěn Kèqīng imposed heavy taxes and levies to please his superiors,
along with the Grand Market Director Yáng Huìlǎng, the Legal Supervisor Xú Xī, and the Departmental Clerk Jì Huì, all of whom harmed the people,
he had them executed below the Stone Tower,
to apologize to the Sānwú region.
He ordered Gāo Jiǒng and the records officer of the Marshal's Office, Péi Jǔ,
to collect maps and registers,
seal the government storehouses,
taking not a single item of wealth,
and all under heaven praised Guǎng for his virtue.
Jǔ
was the younger brother of Ràngzhī.
Péi Ràngzhī appears in the 158th scroll, in the fourth year of the Dàtóng era of Emperor Wǔ of Liáng.
Guǎng, because Hèruò Bì had engaged in decisive battle ahead of schedule,
violating military orders,
arrested him and handed him over to the officials.
The Emperor sent a post-horse summons for him,
and issued an edict to Guǎng, saying:
"The pacification of Jiāngbiǎo
was due to the efforts of Bì and Hán Qínhǔ."
He bestowed upon them ten thousand bolts of silk;
and also bestowed an edict upon Bì and Qínhǔ,
praising their achievements.
Wang Ban, the Pillar of State and Commandant with Equal Honor to the Three Excellencies,
who was the son of Wang Sengbian,
at night,
opened the tomb of Emperor Gaozu of Chen,
burned the bones to ashes,
and threw them into water to drink.
This was to avenge his father.
The incident of Emperor Gaozu of Chen killing Wang Sengbian is recorded in the 166th scroll, in the first year of the Shaotai era of Emperor Jing of Liang.
He was charged with the crime by Prince Guang of Jin;
Prince Guang reported it,
and the Emperor ordered him pardoned.
An edict was issued that the tombs of Emperor Gaozu, Emperor Shizu, and Emperor Gaozong of Chen
should be allocated a total of five households to guard them separately.
The Emperor sent an envoy to inform Xǔ Shànxīn of the fall of Chen,
and Xǔ Shànxīn, wearing mourning clothes, wailed beneath the western steps,
sitting on straw facing east for three days;
last year, Chen had sent Xǔ Shànxīn as an envoy,
and he was detained at the guesthouse,
not allowed to return,
as recorded in the previous scroll.
The western steps
are the steps for guests.
Wearing mourning clothes and sitting on straw
are mourning rites.
Cuī (mourning clothes),

3. Xiǎo Huán, the Chen Dynasty's Governor of Wúzhōu, was able to win the hearts of the people.
After the fall of the Chen Dynasty,
the people of Wú supported Huán as their leader.

As Shù's army was about to arrive,

(Bāo Mountain,

Yuán Xié, the Duke of Lè'ān, advanced and said:

On the day Xīnyǒu,
Yáng Sù was promoted to the rank of Duke of Yuè,
according to the Suí Shū,

Hèruò Bì and Hán Qínhǔ contended over merit before the Emperor.
Bì said:
"I fought desperately at Jiǎngshān,

Qínhǔ said:

The Emperor said:

The officials impeached Qínhǔ for allowing his soldiers to run wild,

sàn,

Alas,

is the name of a mountain.
In ancient times, when Yǔ controlled the floodwaters,

surrounding the mountain as it passed.
The mountain appeared in the water like a pillar,

the water flowed in separate streams.

it is also called Sānmén (Three Gates).

The Emperor also sent Vice Gentleman-in-Attendance Hé Chóu to recruit troops to suppress Guāngshì,
Chóu persuaded Mò Chóng and others to surrender,
and by imperial authority appointed the leaders as prefectural and county officials.
Chóu,
was the nephew of Tuǒ.
The Emperor, because the Lǐngnán barbarians and Yuè people rebelled frequently,
appointed Biàn Prefect Línghú Xī as Guì Prefecture Commander of seventeen prefectures' military affairs,
allowing him to act according to circumstances,
with authority to appoint officials below the prefect level.
Xī arrived at his post,
broadly extended grace and trust,
the stream and cave chieftains said to each other:
"Previous commanders all used military force to coerce us,
now he instructs us with personal edicts,
how can we disobey!"
So they submitted one after another.
Previously, the prefectures and counties were obstinate,
many senior officials could not take up their posts,
governing from the commander's office,
Xī sent them all to their posts,
building cities and towns,
establishing schools,
and both Huá and barbarians were influenced.
The Lǐ chieftain
Níng Měnglì,
had occupied Hǎinán since the Chén era,
Suí pacified and appeased him,
appointing him as Ān Prefect.
Měnglì, relying on the terrain, was arrogant and aloof,
never paying respects,
Xī instructed him with grace and trust,
Měnglì was moved,
went to the office to pay respects,
and dared not act wrongly.
Xī memorialized to change Ān Prefecture to Qīn Prefecture.
Suí Records: Níngyuè Commandery,
established as Ān Prefecture during the Liáng,
now changed to Qīn Prefecture.
4. The Emperor, because subordinate officials everywhere did not respect and fear their superiors,
making affairs difficult to accomplish,
in the third month,
on the day Rénchén,
issued an edict
"When various offices judge subordinate officials' crimes,
if the law is light but the circumstances severe,
they may, beyond the law, consider administering caning."
Thus, superiors and subordinates drove each other,
repeatedly carrying out floggings,
considering cruelty as ability,
and law-abiding as cowardice.
The emperor, due to the great number of robbers and bandits,
decreed that anyone who stole even one coin or more would be executed in the marketplace.
In some cases, three people together stole a single melon,
and when the incident was discovered, they were immediately put to death.
As a result, travelers all rose late and lodged early,
fearing they might inadvertently violate the law.
An examination of discrepancies states: The Treatise on Penal Law records
"lodged late,"
so "early" must be an error.
Several men seized an official and said to him:
"Are we people who seek wealth?
We have come only on behalf of those wronged.
Report to the Supreme Sovereign for us: Since ancient times,
in governing the state and establishing laws,
there has never been execution for stealing a single coin.
If you do not report this for us,
we will come again,
and you and your kind will be wiped out!"
When the emperor heard of this,
he suspended this law.
Since ancient times,
there have been crafty and powerful figures in the villages who held officials' shortcomings against them,
but
it was unheard of for them to confront their superiors to this extent.
No wonder there were so many bandits in the final years of Suí.
The wealth of the world
is accumulated coin by coin.
Therefore, in ancient governance,
they sought to make it equitable and close to the people.
Wéi,
read as yú wèi fān.
The ér in "ér wèi," "ér bù," and "ér shǔ"
means "you."
The emperor once, in a fit of anger,
wanted to have someone beaten to death in the sixth month.
The Vice Minister of the Court of Judicial Review, Zhào Chuò from Hédōng, firmly objected:
Under the Suí system: Each of the Nine Courts had one Minister and one Vice Minister.
Hédōng County
was the seat of Hédōng Commandery in Púzhōu.
Shào,
read as shǐ zhào fān.
"In the last month of summer,
heaven and earth nurture the growth of all things;
it is not permissible to execute anyone at this time."
The emperor replied:
"Although the sixth month is said to be a time of growth,
there must still be thunder and lightning at this time;
I act in accordance with heaven,
so what is impermissible!"
He then had the person killed.
Lái Kuàng, a Clerk in the Court of Judicial Review, submitted a memorial saying that the Court of Judicial Review was too lenient in its affairs.
Clerk (zhǎng gù)
is probably the same as the Han dynasty position of zhǎng gù.
In the Táng dynasty, the various ministries, directorates, courts, and directorates all had Clerks,
following the Suí system.
Shàng,
read as shí zhǎng fān.
He was sent each morning to attend the assembly of the Five Ranks.
Qiǎn,
means to send or to cause.
Háng,
read as hù gāng fān.
Jiàn,
read as xián biàn fān.
The emperor sent a trusted minister to investigate and verify,
and initially found no wrongdoing.
The emperor was angry
and ordered Lái Kuàng beheaded.
Zhào Chuò firmly objected,
believing Lái Kuàng did not deserve death.
The emperor brushed his sleeves and entered the inner chambers.
Zhào Chuò falsely declared,
"I am no longer concerned with Lái Kuàng's case,
but have other matters
I have not yet reported."
The emperor ordered him brought into the inner chambers.
Zhào Chuò bowed twice and pleaded:
"I have three capital offenses:
As Vice Minister of the Court of Judicial Review,
I failed to control the Clerk,
allowing Lái Kuàng to violate the emperor's law—
this is the first.
The prisoner did not deserve death,
yet I could not stake my life to argue for him—
this is the second.
I originally had no other matters,
but lied in order to gain entry—
this is the third."
The emperor's expression softened.
As Empress Dúgū was present,
she ordered that Zhào Chuò be given two golden cups of wine,
and the cups were bestowed upon him as well.
Lái Kuàng was thus spared death
and exiled to Guǎngzhōu.
Xiāo Móhē's son, Shì Lüè, rebelled in Jiāngnán.
Xiāo Móhē should have been implicated and punished.
The emperor said:
"Shì Lüè is not yet twenty years old,
what could he possibly accomplish?
Being the son of a famous general,
he was coerced by others."
He therefore pardoned Xiāo Móhē.
Zhào Chuò firmly remonstrated that this was not permissible.
The emperor could not make him yield,
and wanted Zhào Chuò to leave so he could issue the pardon.
He therefore ordered Zhào Chuò to retire for his meal.
Zhào Chuò said:
"My report on the case is not yet settled,
I dare not retire."
The emperor said:
"Let the Court of Judicial Review issue a special pardon for Xiāo Móhē on my behalf!"
He then ordered his attendants to release him.
The Vice Minister of the Ministry of Justice, Xīn Dǎn, once wore crimson trousers,
as custom said it brought good fortune for official advancement.
The emperor considered it sorcery,
and was about to execute him.
Zhào Chuò said:
"The law does not prescribe death for this,
I dare not obey the decree."
The emperor was furious,
saying:
"You care for Xīn Dǎn but not for yourself!"
He ordered Zhào Chuò taken away for execution.
Zhào Chuò said:
"Your Majesty may kill me,
but you must not kill Xīn Dǎn."
When brought to the court hall,
and his clothes removed for execution,
the emperor sent someone to ask Zhào Chuò:
"What do you say now?"
He replied:
"I am single-minded in upholding the law,
I do not fear death."
The emperor brushed his sleeves and went inside.
After a long while,
he released him.
The next day, he apologized to Zhào Chuò,
consoled and encouraged him,
and bestowed upon him three hundred bolts of silk.
At that time, the emperor had prohibited the use of debased coins.
Two men in the market
exchanged debased coins for good ones.
The Military Patrol arrested them and reported it.
The Military Patrol
was under the Left and Right Generals of the Military Patrol,
responsible for day and night patrols, investigation, and arrest of wrongdoers.
Zhào Chuò remonstrated:
"These men's offense warrants caning,
killing them is not lawful."
The emperor said:
"This does not concern you."
Zhào Chuò said:
"Your Majesty, not considering me foolish and ignorant,
placed me in the judicial office.
If you wish to kill people arbitrarily,
how can it not concern me!"
The emperor said:
"When one shakes a large tree and it does not move, one should withdraw."
He replied:
"I hope to move the heart of heaven,
why speak of moving a tree?"
The emperor said again:
"When drinking soup, if it is hot, one sets it aside.

The Emperor’s application of laws became increasingly severe in his later years.
On New Year’s Day, a censor failed to impeach a military officer whose clothing and sword were not in proper order.
The Emperor said:
“You are a censor,
yet you arbitrarily let things pass as you please.”
He ordered the censor executed.
When the Grand Master of Remonstrance, Máo Sīzǔ, protested,
he too was killed.
The Sui dynasty’s Chancellery had seven Grand Masters of Remonstrance.
⿺麥肙
The Director of the Armory was negligent, allowing the courtyard to become overgrown.
The Director of the Armory
was subordinate to the Court of Imperial Sacrifices.
Some officials accepted gifts of horsewhips and parrots from local administrators.
When the Emperor discovered this,
he personally oversaw their executions.
The Emperor’s moods of joy and anger were unpredictable,
and he no longer adhered to legal statutes.
He trusted Yáng Sù,
who in turn acted arbitrarily and unfairly.
Yáng Sù had a grudge against the Vice Minister of the Court of Diplomatic Relations, Chén Yán.
Once, while passing through the guesthouse for foreign envoys,
he saw horse dung in the courtyard
and servants gambling on a felt rug.
He reported this to the Emperor.
The Emperor was furious.
The Director of Receptions and the gamblers were all beaten to death with clubs,
and Chén Yán was nearly flogged to death.
According to the Sui Records: the Court of Diplomatic Relations oversaw the Director of Receptions,
which is the same as the Director of Guests.
Dung,
pronounced shǐ,
means excrement.
Flogged,
pronounced chuí.
Nearly,
pronounced jī,
also pronounced qí.
The Emperor sent the Grand Commandant of the Personal Guard, Qūtū Tōng of Cháng’ān, to Lǒngxī to inspect the horse pastures.
The Sui established the Left and Right Personal Guards, Left and Right Meritorious Guards, and Left and Right Protective Guards,
with ranks such as Grand Commandant, Commandant, and Adjutant.
Emperor Yáng later changed Grand Commandant to Commandant,
Commandant to Brigade Leader,
and Adjutant to Squad Leader.
Qūtū
is a non-Han compound surname.
Their ancestors were from Tūhé in Chānglí
and later moved to Cháng’ān.
Lǒngxī Commandery
was in Wèi Prefecture.
Qū,
pronounced jiǔ wù.
The Emperor was furious
and intended to execute the Minister of the Imperial Stud, Mùróng Xìdá, and 1,500 supervising officials.
The Minister of the Imperial Stud
was responsible for the administration of livestock,
hence the Emperor wanted to punish them.
“Human life is of utmost importance.
How can Your Majesty kill over a thousand people over livestock?
I dare to plead with my life!”
The Emperor glared and rebuked him.
Qūtū Tōng kowtowed again and said:
“I am willing to die,
but I beg Your Majesty to spare the lives of these thousand people.”
The Emperor was moved to realization,
saying:
“It is my lack of clarity
that has led to this!
I rely on your loyal words.”
Thus, Mùróng Xìdá and the others were spared from death,
and Qūtū Tōng was promoted to General of the Left Martial Guard.
According to the Sui Records: the Left and Right Martial Guards
were responsible for escorting the imperial carriage,
leading the vanguard and guarding the rear,
patrolling day and night,
arresting wrongdoers,
managing beacon towers and roads,
and overseeing water and forage supplies.
During imperial tours and military campaigns,
they enforced camp regulations.
5 The Pillar of State
Liú Chǎng was an old acquaintance of the Emperor
and was held in high favor.
His son, Jūshì,
was chivalrous but disregarded laws and regulations,
frequently committing offenses.
Because of Liú Chǎng,
the Emperor often pardoned him.
Jūshì grew increasingly arrogant and unrestrained.
He would seize robust sons of high officials
and bring them to his home,
placing a cartwheel around their necks and beating them with clubs.
Those who nearly died without yielding
were hailed as brave men,
released, and befriended.
He had a gang of three hundred followers
who assaulted passersby,
committing numerous acts of plunder.
Even high-ranking officials and nobles
dared not confront them.
When it was reported that Jūshì was plotting rebellion,
the Emperor was enraged
and had him executed.
Many sons of high officials were implicated and stripped of their positions.
6 Yáng Sù, Niú Hóng, and others again recommended Zhāng Zhòuxuán’s calendrical expertise.
The previous year, the Emperor had summoned and rewarded Zhāng Zhòuxuán,
but later dismissed him.
Again,
pronounced fú yòu.
There were long-standing difficulties with the old methods,
so the Emperor ordered Liú Huī and others to debate with Zhāng Zhòuxuán and his colleagues.
Liú Huī remained silent and could not answer,
while Zhāng Zhòuxuán resolved fifty-four issues.
The Emperor then appointed Zhāng Zhòuxuán as an Extraordinary Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary and concurrently Grand Astrologer,
awarding him a thousand bolts of silk,
and ordered him to participate in revising the new method.
Extraordinary,
pronounced sǎn.
Cavalier,
pronounced jì.
Zhāng Zhòuxuán completed the calendar.
In summer,
the fourth month,
on the wùyín day,
an edict was issued promulgating the new calendar.
The four previous calendar makers, including Liú Huī, were all stripped of their positions.
7 In autumn, the seventh month,
Lǐ Shìxián of Guì Prefecture rebelled,
and the Emperor discussed launching a campaign.
Several generals volunteered,
but the Emperor refused,
turning instead to the Great General of the Right Martial Guard, Yú Qìngzé, saying:
“You hold the position of chancellor,
with the noble rank of Senior Duke.
At the beginning of the Kāihuáng era,
Qìngzé served as Vice Director of the Right of the Department of State Affairs,
a chancellor’s duty.
He was granted the title of Pillar of State,
enfeoffed as Duke of Lǔ,
a Senior Duke.
Yet you show no intention of going.
Why is that?”
Yú Qìngzé bowed in apology,
filled with fear,
and was then appointed Commander-in-Chief of the Guì Prefecture Campaign,
suppressing the rebellion.
8 The Prince of Qín, Yǒng,
was benevolent and tolerant from a young age
and fond of Buddhism.
He once requested to become a monk,
but was not permitted.
When he became the Area Commander of Bīng Prefecture,
(Yǒng’s appointment as Area Commander of Bīng Prefecture is recorded in the tenth year of the previous volume.)
he violated regulations
by extravagantly constructing palaces.
Yǒng was fond of women,
and his consort, Cuī shì,
sister of Cuī Hóngdù,
was jealous by nature.
She poisoned a melon and served it to him,
causing him to fall ill.
He was recalled to the capital.
The Emperor, considering him extravagant and unrestrained,
on the dīnghài day,
stripped Yǒng of his official position,
allowing him to remain a prince but confining him to his residence.
Cuī shì, for poisoning the prince,
was deposed and cut off,
and ordered to commit suicide at home.
General of the Left Martial Guard, Liú Shēng,
(The position of General of the Martial Guard was established in the Cao Wei period.
From the Jin to the Northern Qi,
it was subordinate to the Left and Right Guards.
It was only in the Sui that it became one of the twelve guard commands alongside the Left and Right Guards.)
said: “The Prince of Qín has committed no other fault
beyond using government resources
to construct official residences.
I believe he can be forgiven.”
The Emperor said:
“The law cannot be violated.”
Yáng Sù remonstrated:
“The Prince of Qín’s offenses
do not warrant such punishment.
I beg Your Majesty to reconsider!”
The Emperor said:
“I am the father of five sons.
(The Emperor’s five sons: Crown Prince Yǒng, Prince of Jìn Guǎng, Prince of Qín Yǒng, Prince of Shǔ Xiù, and Prince of Hàn Liàng.)
If I followed your opinion,
why not create separate laws for the sons of the Son of Heaven?
Even with the virtue of the Duke of Zhōu,
he still executed Guǎn and Cài.
I am far inferior to the Duke of Zhōu,
how can I undermine the law?”
In the end, he did not relent.
Yáng Sù was one who pandered to the ruler’s faults.
Later, he supported the decision to depose Yǒng and install Guǎng,
likely having foreseen this.
In the end,
pronounced zǐ xù.
On the 9th day of the Wùxū cycle,
Tūjué's Tūlì Kèhán came to receive the bride.
The Emperor housed him at the Tàicháng Temple,
where he was instructed in the Six Rites.
The Six Rites are:

Nàcǎi (betrothal gift), Wènmíng (asking the name), Nàjí (announcing the divination), Nàzhēng (sending the betrothal gifts), Qǐngqī (requesting the date), and Qīnyíng (the groom personally fetching the bride).
The Emperor wished to sow discord with Dōulán,
so he deliberately treated him with exceptional courtesy,
dispatching Tàicháng Qīng Niú Hóng, Nàyán Sū Wēi, and Mínbù Shàngshū Húlǜ Xiàoqīng successively as envoys.
In the third year of the Kāihuáng era,
the Dùzhī Shàngshū was renamed Mínbù Shàngshū.
Shǐ (envoy),
is pronounced with the falling tone.
Tūlì originally resided in the north.
After marrying the princess,
Chángsūn Shèng persuaded him to lead his people southward,
settling at the old fortress of Dùjīn.
The old fortress of Dùjīn,
was likely Dūjīn Mountain,
the former residence of Tūjué's Shābōlüè.
Shuài (to lead),
is pronounced as lǜ.
Dōulán angrily said:
the Great Kèhán,
am actually inferior to Rǎngān!"
From then on, his tribute missions ceased,
and he repeatedly came to raid and plunder the border regions.
Tūlì, observing and learning of his movements,
would promptly send reports to the court,
thus the border regions were often prepared in advance.
In the 10th month, on the Jiǎshēn day,
the Emperor returned from the Rénshòu Palace.
When Hé Chóu returned from Lǐngnán,
(in the second month of this year,
Hé Chóu was sent to suppress Lǐngnán).
Chóu, seeing that his illness was severe,
sent him back to Qīnzhōu,
making an agreement with him, saying:
"Between the eighth and ninth months,
you may come to the capital to meet."
The envoy returned,
reported the situation,
and the Emperor was displeased.
In winter,
the tenth month,
Měnglì died of illness.
The Emperor said to Chóu:
"You previously did not bring Měnglì here,
and now he has died after all!"
Chóu said:
"Měnglì made an agreement with your servant:
should he die,
he would send his son to serve at court.
The Yuè people are straightforward by nature,
his son will certainly come."
On his deathbed, Měnglì
indeed admonished his son Chángzhēn, saying:
"I made an agreement with the Grand Envoy,
we must not break our word.
After you bury me,
you should immediately set out on the journey."
Chángzhēn succeeded him as Cìshǐ,
and as promised, came to court.
The Emperor was greatly pleased, saying:
"Hé Chóu's trustworthiness among the barbarians
has reached such a level!"
When Lǔgōng Yú Qìngzé was sent to suppress Lǐ Shìxián,
he appointed his brother-in-law Zhào Shénzhù as his Suífǔ Zhǎngshǐ.
Shénzhù had an affair with Qìngzé's favorite concubine,
and fearing the affair would be exposed,
he spread rumors that Qìngzé was unwilling to undertake this campaign.
When the Emperor heard of this,
the rewards and gifts he bestowed were very meager.
Upon Qìngzé's return,
when he reached Línguì Ridge in Tánzhōu,
(the biography of Yú Qìngzé in the Suí Shū records it as
"Línguì Ridge in Tánzhōu").
Sòng Bái said: After the Suí pacified Chén,
they changed Xiāngzhōu to Tánzhōu.
Dù Yòu said: It was named after Zhāotán.
He said:
"This place is truly rugged and secure,
and with ample provisions,
if defended by the right person,
it would be impregnable to attack."
He sent Shénzhù galloping to the capital to report on affairs,
to observe the Emperor's countenance.
Shénzhù then accused Qìngzé of plotting rebellion.
The Emperor ordered the relevant officials to investigate and verify.
In the twelfth month, on the Rénzǐ day,
Qìngzé was found guilty and executed,
and Shénzhù was appointed Zhùguó.
Gāolì King Tāng, upon hearing of Chén's destruction,
was greatly afraid,
trained troops and stockpiled grain,
preparing a strategy of resistance and defense.
That year,
the Emperor bestowed upon Tāng an imperial edict,
reproaching him for
"although claiming vassalage and allegiance,
his sincerity and integrity were incomplete."
And further said:
"That land of yours,
although its territory is narrow and its people few,
if We now depose you, King,
We cannot leave the position vacant;
ultimately, We must select another official
to go there and pacify the region.
If you, King, cleanse your heart and change your conduct,
and fully abide by the laws and regulations,
then you shall be Our loyal minister.
Why would We need to trouble Ourselves to dispatch another talented individual?
You, King, speak of the breadth of the Liáo River;
how does it compare to the Yangtze River?
The people of Gāolì,
how many are they compared to the state of Chén?
If We did not cherish nurturing and tolerance,
and held you, King, accountable for your past faults,
dispatching a single general
would require no great effort!
We earnestly explain and make this clear,
allowing you, King, to reform yourself."
Tāng received the letter,
was terrified,
and was about to submit a memorial expressing his apology.
He then fell ill and died.
His son Yuán succeeded him.
The Emperor sent an envoy to appoint Yuán as Shàngkāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī,
inheriting the title of Duke of Liáodōng.
Shǐ shǐ (to send an envoy),
is pronounced with the falling tone;
the same applies below.
He then requested to be enfeoffed as king,
and the Emperor granted it.
From that time on, the Suí dynasty remained concerned about Gāolì,
and later, due to its fondness for military campaigns, it ultimately perished.
Tǔyùhún was in great turmoil.
Tǔ,
is pronounced with the entering tone.
Yù,
is pronounced yù.
They established his younger brother Fúyǔn as ruler,
and sent an envoy to explain the matter of the deposition and succession,
and to apologize for the crime of acting without authorization,
also requesting, according to custom, to marry a princess;
the Emperor consented.
From then on, tribute missions arrived yearly.
In spring,
the second month,
on the Jiǎchén day,
the Emperor visited the Rénshòu Palace.
Gāolì King Yuán led over ten thousand Mòhé troops to raid Liáoxī.
The Suí Shū states: The Mòhé are north of Gāolì,
comprising seven tribes: the first is called the Lìmò tribe,
bordering Gāolì;
the second is called the Bóduō tribe,
north of Lìmò;
the third is called the Ānchēgǔ tribe,
northeast of Bóduō;
the fourth is called the Fúniè tribe,
east of Bóduō;
the fifth is called the Hàoshì tribe,
east of Fúniè;
the sixth is called the Hēishuǐ tribe,
northwest of Ānchēgǔ;
the seventh is called the Báishān tribe,
southeast of Lìmò.
Among them, the Hēishuǐ tribe was particularly strong and vigorous,
being the ancient Sùshèn people.
Liáoxī Commandery's seat was at Liǔchéng;
the Suí established the Yíngzhōu Zǒngguǎn Fǔ there.
Mò,
is pronounced mò.
Hé,
is pronounced hé.
When the Emperor heard this, he was furious.
On the Yǐsì day,
he appointed Hànwáng Liàng and Wáng Shìjī jointly as Xíngjūn Yuánshuài,
to lead a land and naval force of three hundred thousand to attack Gāolì,
with Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè Gāo Jiǒng as Hànwáng's Zhǎngshǐ,
and Zhōu Luóhóu as Shuǐjūn Zǒngguǎn.
3. Yánzhōu Cìshǐ Dúgū Tuó.
Suíshū: Yán'ān Commandery,
established as Dōngxiàzhōu during the Later Wèi,
renamed Yánzhōu during the Western Wèi.
Tuó,
pronunciation: tú hé.
He practiced cat demon magic,
which could be used to kill people.
It was said that whenever someone was killed,
the wealth of the deceased's family would secretly transfer to the household that kept the cat demon.
It happened that both Empress Dúgū and Yáng Sù's wife, Lady Zhèng, fell ill.
The physicians all said:
"It is the cat demon illness."
The Suíshū biography of Tuó states: Xú Āní practiced cat demon magic.
She would make offerings to it every midnight.
The term 'midnight' refers to
the hour of the rat.
Tuó once asked for wine from his household,
and his wife said:
"There is no money to buy it."
Tuó then said to Āní: You can send the cat demon to Yuè Gōng's house,
so that I have enough money.
Āní then cast a spell.
After several days,
the cat demon went to Sù's house.
In the eleventh year,
when the Emperor had just returned from Bìngzhōu,
Tuó said to Āní:
"You can send the cat demon to the Empress's place,
so that she bestows many things upon me."
Āní cast the spell again,
and it entered the palace.
The Dàlǐchéng Yáng Yuǎn then had Āní summoned at the outer bureau of the Ménxiàshěng to call forth the cat demon.
Āní then placed a bowl of fragrant porridge that night,
tapped it with a spoon and called out:
"Cat maiden, you may come,
do not stay in the palace."
After a long time,
Āní's face turned bluish-green,
as if she were being pulled.
She said the cat demon had arrived.
From this, the full truth of the matter was obtained.
To keep/raise,
pronunciation: xū yù;
same below.
The Empress's half-brother,
Tuó's wife,
was Yáng Sù's half-sister.
Because of this, they suspected Tuó was responsible.
They ordered Gāo Jiǒng and others to jointly investigate the case.
The full truth was obtained.
The Emperor was angry.
He ordered Tuó and his wife to be placed in an ox-cart,
intending to have them executed.
Empress Dúgū fasted for three days,
pleading for their lives, saying:
"If Tuó had harmed governance and the people,
I would not dare speak;
but now he is in trouble because of me,
I dare to plead for his life."
Tuó's younger brother, the Sīxūn Shìláng Zhěng, went to the palace to beg for mercy.
The Sīxūn Shìláng was under the Minister of Personnel.
(Tuó) was stripped of his official status and made a commoner.
His wife, Lady Yáng, was made a nun.
Previously,
someone had accused (someone) of their mother being killed by a cat demon.
The Emperor considered it superstitious nonsense,
became angry, and sent them away.
At this point,
an edict was issued to execute the accused family that practiced cat demon magic.
Summer,
fourth month,
Xīnhài day,
an edict stated:
"Households that keep cat demons, practice gu poison, evil charms, or wild sorcery,
Suíshū records: In the various commanderies south of the Yangtze, keeping gu was common,
and Yíchūn was particularly severe.
The method involves gathering a hundred kinds of insects on the fifth day of the fifth month,
the largest being snakes,
the smallest being lice.
They are placed together in a vessel,
left to devour each other.
The one remaining species is kept.
If it is a snake, it is called snake gu;
if a louse, louse gu.
It is used to kill people.
By entering a person's stomach through food,
it eats their five viscera.
When the person dies, their property transfers to the gu master's household.
If no one is killed for three years,
the keeper himself will suffer the harm.
It is passed down through generations of descendants without end,
and can also accompany a woman when she marries.
Charm/curse,
pronunciation: yǎn.
Evil spirit,
pronunciation: mèi.
4. Sixth month,
Bǐngyín day,
an edict was issued deposing Gāolì King Yuán from his official titles and ranks.
Prince of Hàn, Liàng's army marched out of Línyú Pass.
Línyú Pass
is located 480 li west of Liǔchéng,
the so-called peril of Lúlóng.
Yú,
Hànshū pronunciation: yù.
Supply transport could not keep up,
the army ran short of food,
and furthermore encountered pestilence.
Zhōu Luóhóu sailed from Dōnglái across the sea towards Píngrǎng City.
Suíshū: Píngrǎng City is six li from east to west,
winding with the mountains,
facing the Pèishuǐ river to the south.
Dù Yòu said: Píngrǎng City is the old Wángxiǎn City of the Cháoxiǎn state.
To head towards,
pronunciation: qù.
Many ships were lost at sea.
Autumn,
ninth month,
Jǐchǒu day,
the army returned,
eight or nine out of ten had died.
Gāolì King Yuán also, in fear, sent an envoy to apologize and admit guilt,
submitting a memorial calling himself
"Your servant from the dung and soil of Liáodōng, Yuán."
The Emperor then ceased military action,
treating him as before.
The King of Bǎijì, Chāng, sent an envoy presenting a memorial,
requesting to serve as a military guide.
The Emperor issued an edict instructing him that
"Gāolì has submitted and admitted guilt,
We have already pardoned them,
so an attack cannot be launched."
He treated the envoy generously and sent him back.
Gāolì learned quite a bit about this matter,
and sent troops to raid their territory.
5. Xīnmǎo day,
the Emperor arrived from Rénshòu Palace.
6. Winter,
eleventh month,
Guǐwèi day,
the Emperor performed the suburban sacrifice to Heaven in the southern suburb.
7. Twelfth month,
from the capital to Rénshòu Palace,
twelve traveling palaces were established.
8. The Nánníng barbarian Cuàn Wán rebelled again.
Prince of Shǔ, Xiù, memorialized that
"Shǐ Wànsuì accepted bribes and let the bandits go,
causing border troubles to arise."
The Emperor reprimanded Wànsuì.
Wànsuì denied the charges;
the Emperor was angry,
and ordered him executed.
Gāo Jiǒng and Left Guard General-in-Chief Yuán Mín and others firmly pleaded, saying:
"Wànsuì's bold strategies surpass others,
officers and soldiers gladly exert themselves for him.
Even ancient famous generals
could not surpass him."
The Emperor's anger lessened somewhat.
Thereupon, (Wànsuì) was stripped of his official status and made a commoner.
1. Spring,
first month,
Guǐyǒu day,
a general amnesty was declared in the realm.
2. Second month,
Jiǎyín day,
the Emperor visited Rénshòu Palace.
Rénshòu Palace was completed in the 15th year of the Kāihuáng era.
When it was completed,
Emperor Wén was angry,
intending to punish Yáng Sù.
Empress Dúgū was pleased and rewarded him.
Following this, (the Emperor) frequently visited Rénshòu Palace.
By the end of the Rénshòu era,
he eventually died at Rénshòu Palace.
The benevolent enjoy longevity.
The Emperor exhausted the people's strength to build a detached palace.
Can this be called benevolent?
That he did not meet his death in this palace
is fitting.
The Emperor was angry with Yáng Sù but did not punish him;
when his empress was pleased, he then also followed in being pleased.
Was it not that luxury and extravagance can change a person?
Stimulated by the surroundings,
to the point of lingering and not knowing to turn back,
he ultimately left a legacy of laughter for ten thousand generations.
From this we know that for a ruler's virtue, frugality is precious.
3 The Tūjué Tūlì Kèhán, through Chángsūn Shèng, reported that the Dūlán Kèhán was preparing siege weapons,
intending to attack the Great Harmony City.
According to the Táng Records: from Xiàzhōu, cross the Wūshuǐ to the north,
travel over 530 lǐ,
pass Héngshuǐ,
then travel another 119 lǐ to reach Ānlè Garrison.
The garrison is on the west bank of the river,
and on the east bank lies the ancient Great Harmony City.
The present-day Great Harmony City
is the ancient Yǒngjì Barrier.
Jué,
read as jiǔ wù fān.
Kè,
read with the entering tone from kān.
Hán,
read as hán.
Cháng,
read as zhī liǎng fān.
Shèng,
read as chéng zhèng fān.
The Minister of the Left, Gāo Jiǒng, marched out via the Shuòzhōu route.
According to the Suí Records: Mǎyì Commandery
was formerly established as Shuòzhōu.
Língwǔ Commandery
was established as Língzhōu during the Later Wèi.
All were placed under the command of the Prince of Hàn;
however, the Prince of Hàn ultimately did not take to the field.
Dūlán, upon hearing this,
formed an alliance with the Dátóu Kèhán,
combined their forces, and launched a surprise attack on Tūlì.
A great battle ensued at the foot of the Great Wall,
and Tūlì was utterly defeated.
Dūlán slaughtered all of Tūlì's brothers, sons, and nephews,
then crossed the river and entered Yùzhōu.
According to the Suí Records: Língqiū County in Yànmén Commandery
had Yùzhōu established there during the Later Zhōu.
Yù,
read as yū wù fān.
At night,
Tūlì, along with Chángsūn Shèng, fled south with five horsemen.
By dawn,
they had traveled over a hundred lǐ,
and gathered several hundred horsemen.
Tūlì consulted with his subordinates, saying:
"Now that we are defeated and entering the court,
we are merely surrendered men.
Would the Suí Emperor treat us with courtesy?
Although Diànjué has come,
there was originally no grievance or enmity between us.
Yuān,
means resentment.
He is sure to provide for us."
Shèng, aware of this,
secretly sent a messenger into Fúyuǎn Garrison,
ordering them to quickly light the beacon fires.
Tūlì saw all four beacons lit,
and asked Shèng about it.
Shèng deceived him, saying:
"The city is high and the land vast,
they must have seen the enemy approaching from afar.
According to our state's regulations,
if the enemy is few,
two beacons are lit;
if they come in greater numbers,
three beacons are lit;
if they are pressing close in large force,
four beacons are lit.
They see that the enemy is numerous and close by."
Tūlì was greatly frightened,
and said to his men:
"The pursuing troops are already upon us,
we had better take refuge in the city."
Once they entered the garrison,
Shèng left Tūlì's senior official, Zhíshì, in charge of the troops,
and personally escorted Tūlì by post-horse to the court.
Jiàng,
read with its usual pronunciation.
In the fourth month,
on Dīngyǒu,
Tūlì arrived at Cháng'ān.
The Emperor was greatly pleased,
and appointed Shèng as General of the Left Meritorious Guard and Piàoqí General.
Suí regulations: Piàoqí General is rank 4a.
Piào,
read as pì miào fān.
Qí,
read as qí jì fān.
The Emperor ordered Tūlì and Dūlán's envoy, Yīntóu Tèlè, to confront and interrogate each other.
Tūlì's arguments were just,
so the Emperor treated him generously.
Dūlán's younger brother, Yù
Sùliù, abandoned his wife and children,
and came to the court with Tūlì.
The Emperor praised him,
and had Tūlì bestow many treasures upon him to console his heart.
Gāo Jiǒng sent the Supreme Pillar of State, Zhào Zhòngqīng, to lead three thousand troops as the vanguard.
They reached Zúlǐ Mountain,
encountered the Tūjué,
fought for seven days,
and inflicted a major defeat upon them;
pursued them in flight to Qǐfú Marsh,
defeated them again,
capturing over a thousand people,
and tens of thousands of various livestock.
The Tūjué returned in great force,
Zhòngqīng formed a square formation,
resisting and fighting on all sides,
for a total of five days.
When Gāo Jiǒng's main army arrived,
they joined in the attack,
the Tūjué were defeated and fled,
they were pursued across the Báidào,
and chased over seven hundred lǐ beyond Qín Mountain before returning.
Yáng Sù's army encountered Dátóu.
Previously, when various generals fought the Tūjué,
fearing their cavalry charges,
they all intermixed war chariots, infantry, and cavalry,
setting up deer antlers to form a square formation,
with the cavalry inside.
This was an ancient method,
not even Wèi Qīng or Liú Yù could change it,
the so-called 'first make oneself invincible, then wait for the enemy to become vulnerable.'
Xiān,
read as xī jiàn fān.
Qí,
read as qí jì fān;
same below.
"This is merely a method for self-preservation,
insufficient for achieving victory."
Thereupon, he completely abolished the old methods,
ordering all armies to form cavalry formations.
Dátóu, hearing of this,
said with great joy:
"Heaven has bestowed this upon me!"
He dismounted, looked up to heaven and bowed,
then led over a hundred thousand cavalry straight forward.
The Commandant of the Three Excellencies, Zhōu Luóhóu, said:
"The enemy formation is not yet orderly,
I request to attack them."
He led elite cavalry in a counterattack,
Sù followed with the main army,
the Tūjué were utterly defeated,
Dátóu, severely wounded, fled,
casualties were beyond count,
his troops departed wailing.
Wèi Shū destroyed chariots and exalted infantry to defeat the Dí;
Yáng Sù abolished war chariots and formed cavalry formations to crush the Tūjué;
both achieved victory by striking when the enemy was in disarray.
Shuài,
read as shuài.
Shèng,
read as shēng.
Háo,
read as hù gāo fān.
4 In the sixth month,
on Dīngyǒu,
Yùzhāng Prince Jiǎn was appointed as the Director of the Palace Secretariat.
5 Yíyáng Duke Wáng Shìjī was appointed as Governor of Liángzhōu.
His trusted follower, Huángfǔ Xiàoxié from Āndìng, committed a crime,
Wáng Shìjī was enfeoffed as Duke of Yíyáng Commandery.
According to the Suí Records: Yíyáng County in Hénán Commandery
had Yíyáng Commandery established there during the Later Wèi.
Wǔwēi Commandery
was formerly established as Liángzhōu.
Āndìng Commandery
was formerly established as Jīngzhōu.
He fled to seek refuge with Shìjī,
but Shìjī did not take him in.
Xiàoxié was sentenced to garrison duty in Guìzhōu.
'Pèi fáng' means
to be assigned to the military ranks,
making them perform guard duty.
He claimed
"Shìjī once had a Daoist priest read his fortune to see if he would become noble or not.
The Daoist priest replied: 'You, sir, are destined to become a ruler of a state,
and will also go to Liángzhōu.'
Zhī,
means to go.
Great deeds can be plotted.'
Shìjī said: 'Liángzhōu has vast land but sparse population,
it is not a state suited for military exploits.'"
Shìjī was implicated and executed,

and the enemy did not notice them.

inflicting a major defeat on them,
and recovered all the people and livestock to return to Qǐmín.
From then on, the Tūjué fled far away,
and there were no more raids south of the desert.
For 磧,

For 抄,

Xuán Zòng was enfeoffed as Duke of Huáinán.
Duke of the Huáinán Commandery.

Collected works,

Guāzi

Earlier,

Minor,

Sù, relying on his high status,

Yíngzhōu had the Huáiyuǎn city.

forgetting his minor faults.

Jiāozhōu.
Lǐ,
pronounced lǐ.

1. In autumn,
the eighth month,
on the Rénshēn day,
Yān Róng, the Area Commander of Yōuzhōu, was ordered to commit suicide.
Róng was by nature severe and cruel,
whipping his attendants
often up to a thousand lashes.
Once, seeing thorny bushes by the roadside,

and immediately tried them on people.
If someone pleaded innocence,

Hóng once casually asked Xuàn:
"Under the Zhōu rituals, there were many scholars but few clerks.
Now the number of clerks is a hundred times greater than before;
reducing them would not suffice—what is the reason for this?"
Xuàn said:
"The ancients delegated authority and held people accountable for results,
assessing their performance at year's end.
Cases were not repeatedly reviewed,
documents were not excessively detailed;
the duty of clerks was merely to manage key items.
Nowadays, documents and records are constantly worried over for reexamination.
If the investigation is not thorough,
evidence may be sought from ten thousand lǐ away for cases a hundred years old.
Hence the proverb: 'Old clerks die clutching their case files.'
The complexity of affairs and the maladministration stem from this."
Hóng said:

even the slightest trace of conduct
falls under the jurisdiction of the Bureau of Evaluation.

is in charge of assessing the merits, faults, conduct, and abilities of all civil and military officials, both internal and external,

Hóng thought his words were good but could not implement them.

1 In spring,
the first month,
on the yǐsì day,
an edict was issued to mobilize over a million troops from Héběi to dig the Yǒngjì Canal,
drawing water from the Qìn River south to the Yellow River,
and north to Zhuō Commandery.
*Bǎn Zhì*: The Qìn River originates from Yángtóu Mountain, Shìmǐ Valley, in Gǔyuǎn County, Shàngdǎng.
Yán Shìgǔ said: It now enters the Yellow River in the area of Wǔzhì County, Huáizhōu.
Gǔyuǎn,
became Qìnyuán County in the Suí dynasty.
Qìn,
pronounced as *qīzhèn*.
*Textual Analysis*: According to *Miscellaneous Records*:
"In the third year, sixth month,
an order was issued to open the Yǒngjì Canal,
leading the Fén River into the Yellow River.
A canal was dug northeast of the Fén River,
connecting the canal water to Zhuō Commandery over two thousand *li*,
to allow passage for dragon boats."
Note: The Yǒngjì Canal is the present-day Imperial River,
which never connected to the Fén River.
*Miscellaneous Records* is mistaken.
Women were first conscripted for labor.

the Emperor dispatched the Attendant Court Greeter Cuī Jūnsù to bear an imperial edict to comfort and instruct him.
The Emperor established the Greeter's Office with one Grand Master,
and established two Attendant Court Greeters to assist him.
Chǔ,
pronounced Chāng Lǚ's fān.
Jué,
pronounced Jiǔ Wù's fān.
Kě,
follows the entering tone of Cóng Kān.
Hán,
pronounced Hán.
Shǐ,

Cháo,
pronounced Zhí Yáo's fān.

"Cuī Yì",
but here we follow the Western Tūjué biography.
Chǔluó received the edict but refused to rise,
so Jūnsù said to him:
"The Tūjué were originally one nation,
which split into two,
fighting each other every year.
For decades, neither could destroy the other,

Yet Qǐmín, leading his tribe of a million people,
humbled himself and bowed low,
submitting as a subject to the Son of Heaven.
What was the reason for this?
Precisely because he deeply hated you, Kèhán,
and being unable to subdue you alone,
wished to borrow troops from the great nation,
to jointly destroy you, Kèhán.
All the ministers wished to grant Qǐmín's request,
and the Son of Heaven had already approved it.
The army's departure was imminent.
However, your mother, Lady Xiàng,
Kě,
follows the entering tone of Cóng Kān.
Hán,
pronounced Hán.
Xiàng,
pronounced Shì Liàng's fān.
day and night guarded the palace gate,
weeping and pleading sorrowfully,
prostrating herself to confess her fault,
begging to send an envoy to summon you, Kèhán,
and have you submit and become an internal dependency.
The Son of Heaven took pity on her,
and therefore sent an envoy here again.
Now you, Kèhán, are acting so arrogant and disrespectful.
Then Lady Xiàng would have deceived the Son of Heaven,
and would certainly be executed in the marketplace,

Barbarian court,

Using the forces of the eastern state,

Chǔluó, startled, rose,

on the day Rénxū,
the King of Wō, Duōlìsībǐgū

5. On the day Yǐchǒu,
the imperial carriage proceeded to Wǔyuán.
The Emperor changed Fēng Prefecture to Wǔyuán Commandery.
It was built last year.
Suí Zhì: When the Emperor toured north beyond the frontier,
the traveling palace was set up with a Liùhé Fortress,
one hundred and twenty paces square,
forty-two chǐ high.
Liùhé,
made of wood,
one chǐ square,
the outer side of each square had boards,
which could be joined or separated,
painted blue.
Six boards were stacked to form a wall,
thirty-six chǐ high,
with a parapet added on top,
the boards six chǐ high,
with north and south gates.
Also, at the four corners of the wall, two watchtowers were erected,
the gate towers and gatehouse railings were all painted with red, blue, and colorful patterns.
Also built were a Liùhé Hall and a thousand-man tent,
carried on spear-carts,
the carts carrying three Liùhé boards.
The cart railings could be disassembled and crossed,
becoming horse spears.
All had canopies spread over the carts,
under the canopies were placed level crossbows with attached arrows,
guarded by five men in shifts.
Between two carts,
cart railings and horse spears were deployed,
all with their shafts facing outward,
forming an outer perimeter.
Inside this, iron caltrops were spread,
further inside, thorny barriers were placed.
In the center, crossbow beds were set up,
six chǐ long,
three chǐ wide;
the bed frames and steps were inserted with steel spikes,
all five cùn long,
called "shrimp whiskers",
all fitted with mechanisms,
when deployed, the spikes all faced outward.
On the beds were placed swivel crossbows,
connected to the crossbow triggers by ropes.
If someone approached from outside,
touched the rope, then the crossbow mechanism would rotate,
and shoot towards the point of contact.
Outside this, tripwires surrounded the traveling palace for two zhàng,
with one bell per post,
the posts holding the tripwires,
two chǐ five cùn off the ground.
At the north and south gates of the traveling palace, hammers and chime stones were installed,
connected to the tripwires,
triggered by mechanisms.
If someone touched a tripwire,
then all the bells would sound,
the hammers would strike the two chime stones,
to alert of the alarm,
called "striking the chime stones".
Textual analysis notes: Zá Jì says,
"When the Emperor visited Qǐmín's tent, a traveling fortress was built,
two thousand paces in circumference,

Here we follow the Suí Lǐyí Zhì.
Each time they stopped to rest,
they would turn the shafts outward to form an outer perimeter,
and spread iron caltrops inside;
Ěryǎ Yì says: Nowadays, armies use iron to make thorns,
to scatter on enemy roads,
called iron caltrops.
Some say: Iron caltrops with sharp angles,
originated when Emperor Yáng campaigned against Liáo.
However, the Liù Tāo already mentions this object,
and Cháo Cuò's biography calls it "qú dá".
All were inserted with steel spikes,
facing outward;
on top were placed swivel crossbows,
connected to the triggers by ropes.
If someone approached and touched the rope,
then the crossbow mechanism would rotate,
and shoot towards the point of contact.
Outside this, tripwires surrounded the area,

otherwise,

Envoy,

7 The emperor never ceased building palaces.
Although there were many gardens, pavilions, and halls in the two capitals and Jiāngdū,
over time he grew increasingly weary of them.
Whenever he traveled on pleasure trips,
looking around left and right,
he found nothing to his liking,
and did not know where to go.
He then demanded maps of all the mountains and rivers in the empire,
personally examined them,
seeking scenic locations suitable for constructing palaces and gardens.
In summer,
the fourth month,
an edict was issued to build the Fényáng Palace
north of Fénzhōu, at the source of the Fén River.
According to the Sui Records: Fényuán County in Lóufán Commandery,
formerly known as Kělán,
was renamed Jìnglè in the fourth year of the Dàyè era,
and had the Fényáng Palace, Guǎncén Mountain, Tiānchí, and the Fén River.
The Records of the Thirteen Provinces states: the Fén River originates from Yānjīng Mountain in Wǔzhōu,
another name for Guǎncén Mountain.
According to the Commentary on the Water Classic,
on Yānjīng Mountain there is a large pool,
commonly called Tiānchí.
Note: Emperor Yáng built the Fényáng Palace encircling Tiānchí,
as detailed later in the commentary on Wǔtái.
8. Initially, when Crown Prince Yuándé passed away,
(see the second year in the previous volume),
the over twenty thousand officials and soldiers under Yuándé
were all transferred to Yǎng.
The Emperor meticulously selected staff for him,
appointing the Junior Minister of the Imperial Stud, Liǔ Jiǎnzhī, as Chief Administrator to the Prince of Qí.
He also admonished him, saying:
"If the Prince of Qí's virtue and achievements are cultivated and complete,
wealth and honor will naturally gather at your family's gate;
(Zhōng means 'to gather').
But if he commits crimes, you will also be implicated."
Jiǎnzhī was the nephew of Liǔ Qìng.
(Liǔ Qìng served under Yǔwén Tài. Cóng is pronounced with the cái yòng fān).
When officials hurried to pay their respects,
the roads were clogged and noisy.
Yǎng became arrogant and unrestrained because of this,
associating closely with petty men,
and many of his actions were unlawful.
He sent his attendants Qiáo Lìngzé and Kùdí Zhòngqí
(Kùdí is a compound surname. Qí is pronounced yú qǐ fān.)
Lìngzé and others thus acted wantonly.
Whenever they heard of a family having a beautiful woman,
they would falsely claim Yǎng's order to summon her,
bring her into Yǎng's residence,
violate her, and then send her away.
Zhòngqí and Zhì Wěi went to Lǒngxī,
torturing various Hu tribesmen,
demanding their famous horses from them.
(The Emperor changed Wèizhōu to Lǒngxī Commandery. Zhuā is pronounced cè guā fān.)
Yǎng ordered them to return the horses to their owners,
but Zhòngqí and others deceitfully said the Prince had bestowed them,
and took them to their own homes.
Yǎng was unaware of this.
The Princess of Lèpíng once reported to the Emperor,
saying that a daughter of the Liǔ family was beautiful.
(The Princess of Lèpíng was the Empress of Emperor Tiānyuán of Zhōu. Lè is pronounced luò.)
After some time,
the Princess again presented the Liǔ woman to Yǎng,
and Yǎng accepted her.
Later, the Emperor asked the Princess:
"Where is the Liǔ woman now?"

The Emperor said to his attending ministers:
