Dàohéng himself believed his offense was not major,
and urged the judicial authorities to conclude the case quickly,
hoping that when the report was submitted, the Emperor would surely pardon him.
He ordered his family to prepare a feast,
to receive guests who might come to inquire.
When the report was submitted,
the Emperor ordered him to commit suicide.
Dàohéng was utterly unprepared for this,
and could not bring himself to do it.
The judicial authorities reported again,
and he was strangled to death.
His wife and children were exiled to Qiěmò.
All under heaven considered it an injustice.
11 The Emperor conducted a grand review of military supplies,
praising the excellence of the weapons and armor.
Yǔwén Shù thereupon remarked:
"This is all the achievement of Yún Dìngxīng."
The Emperor immediately promoted Dìngxīng to the position of Assistant Minister of the Court of the Imperial Treasury.
1 In spring,
the first month,
on the first day, Guǐhài,
before dawn, at three kè,
several tens of bandits,
wearing plain caps and white robes,
burning incense and holding flowers,
claiming to be Maitreya Buddha,
entered through the Jiànguó Gate.
(According to Buddhist teachings,
it is believed that when Śākyamuni Buddha declines,
Maitreya Buddha will appear in the world.
Therefore, bandits claimed this identity to carry out their villainy.
The Jiànguó Gate was likely the Duānmén of the imperial city in the Eastern Capital.
The Táng Liù Diǎn states: In the fifth year of Wǔdé, after pacifying Wáng Shìchōng,
disliking its magnificence,
they burned the Qiányáng Hall and the Jiànguó Gate.
Huā,
is read as "flower.")
Textual analysis notes: The Miscellaneous Records place this in the first month of the fifth year,
and also say
"three hundred people."
Here, we follow the Suí Shū.
They then seized the weapons of the guards,
intending to start a rebellion.
Prince Qí, Jiǎn, encountered and beheaded them.
Thereupon, a great search was conducted in the capital,
implicating over a thousand households.
2 The Emperor, as the chieftains of various foreign tribes had all gathered in Luòyáng,
on Dīngchǒu day,
set up an entertainment ground on Duānmén Street.
(The street outside the Duānmén gate of the Luòyáng imperial city.)
The performance area was five thousand paces in circumference,
with eighteen thousand people playing silk and bamboo instruments,
the sound could be heard for several tens of *lǐ*,
from dusk until dawn,
the lights and torches illuminated heaven and earth;
it lasted for a full month before concluding,
costing an immense sum.
From then on, it became an annual custom.
(Dīngchǒu day
was the fifteenth day of the first month.
The modern practice of celebrating the Lantern Festival
likely began to flourish from this time.) The various foreign tribes requested to enter the Fēngdū Market for trade.
(The eastern market of the Eastern Capital was called Fēngdū,
the southern market was called Dàtóng,
and the northern market was called Tōngyuǎn.)
He first ordered the shops and stores to be renovated and decorated,
making the eaves and buildings uniform,
lavishly displaying curtains and canopies,
with precious goods piled high,
and people splendidly attired.
Even vegetable sellers used Lóngxū mats.
(Lóngxū mats are woven from Lóngxū grass.
Nowadays, many residents of Ānqìng Prefecture in the Huái region are skilled at weaving Lóngxū mats.)
He ordered them all to be invited to sit,
to eat and drink their fill before dispersing,
without charging them.
He deceived them, saying:
"The Central Plains is abundant and prosperous,
it is customary not to charge for wine and food."
The foreign guests were all astonished.
The shrewder among them were somewhat aware of the deception.
Seeing silk fabrics wrapped around trees,
they said:
"The Central Plains also has poor people
whose clothes do not cover their bodies.
Why not give these things to them instead?
What is the point of wrapping trees?"
The market people were ashamed and could not reply.
The Emperor praised Péi Jǔ's capability,
saying to his ministers:
"Péi Jǔ greatly understands my intentions.
All that he presents and reports
are my own settled plans.
Before I have even expressed them,
Jǔ has already reported them to me.
If he were not devoted to the state with all his heart,
who could be like this!"

At that time, Péi Jǔ, along with the Right Flank Guard General-in-Chief Yǔwén Shù, the Vice Director of the Secretariat Yú Shìjī, the Censor-in-Chief Péi Yùn, and the Grand Master of Splendid Happiness Guō Yǎn, all enjoyed favor through flattery and sycophancy.
Shù was adept at serving and attending,
his demeanor and conduct were obsequious,
and all the attendants took him as a model.
Guō Yǎn once advised the Emperor to hold court only once every five days,
saying:
"Do not emulate Gāozǔ,
exhausting yourself in vain."
The Emperor considered him even more loyal,
saying:
"Only Guō Yǎn's heart is the same as mine."
The Emperor appeared dignified and solemn when holding court,
his speeches and issued edicts
were elegant and meaningful in wording and content;
but inwardly he was devoted to sensual pleasures.
When in the two capitals or on inspection tours,
he often had Buddhist monks, nuns, Daoist priests, and female officials accompany him.
(Female officials
were female Daoist priests.)
The Duke of Liáng, Xiāo Jù,
was the nephew of Xiāo Cóng;
the Personal Guard Yǔwén Xiǎo
was the grandson of Yǔwén Qìng.
(According to Suí regulations,
there were twelve Personal Guards of the Left and Right,
responsible for handling the imperial bow and arrows.
Yǔwén Qìng appears in scroll 173, the eleventh year of the Tàijiàn era of Chén Gāozōng.)
(Xiǎo is pronounced with the *hù* and *liǎo* fanqie spellings.)
Every day, the Emperor would set out lavish feasts of wine and food in the pavilions and groves of the imperial park,
ordering Prince Yàn, Dàn, along with Jù, Xiǎo, and the consorts of Gāozǔ to sit at one table,
the monks, nuns, Daoist priests, and female officials at another table,
and himself with his various favorite concubines at yet another table,
the tables roughly connected.
After court was dismissed, he would immediately join them.
They feasted and drank, urging each other on,
becoming intoxicated and disorderly,
with no limit to their excesses,
and this became the norm.
Beautiful women of the Yáng clan
were often presented for the Emperor's pleasure.
Xiǎo came and went from the palace women's quarters,
unrestricted by gates or prohibitions.
As for the imperial concubines and princesses, there were scandalous rumors,
but the Emperor did not punish him for it.
3 The Emperor again sent Zhū Kuān to pacify and recruit Liúqiú.
Liúqiú did not submit,
so the Emperor sent the Tiger Guard General Chén Léng of Lújiāng and the Court Consultant Zhāng Zhènzhōu of Tóng'ān to mobilize over ten thousand troops from Dōngyáng
and sail from Yì'ān to attack them.
After traveling for over a month,
they reached their country,
with Zhènzhōu as the vanguard.
The King of Liúqiú, Kělàdōu,
sent troops to meet them in battle;
they were repeatedly defeated,
and [the Suí forces] reached their capital.
(The residence of the King of Liúqiú was called the Póluótán Cave,
with three layers of trenches and palisades,
surrounded by flowing water,
and thorny trees forming a fence.)
They were defeated again
and retreated into the palisade;
Léng and others took advantage of the victory to attack and capture it,
beheading Kělàdōu,
and capturing over ten thousand of his people before returning.
In the second month,
on Yǐsì day,
Léng and others presented the captives from Liúqiú.
Rewards were distributed to all officials,
Léng was promoted to the position of Right Grand Master of Splendid Happiness,
and Zhènzhōu to Grand Master of the Golden Seal and Purple Ribbon.
4 On Yǐmǎo day,
an edict was issued stating:
"In recent times, noble titles have been recklessly bestowed,
with names and realities at odds.
From now on, only those with meritorious achievements shall be granted enfeoffment,
and it shall still be ordered that their descendants inherit."
Consequently, the previously bestowed five ranks of nobility
were all revoked from those without merit.
5 On Gēngshēn day,
the miscellaneous entertainers conscripted from the Zhōu, Qí, Liáng, and Chén
were all assigned to the Tàicháng Temple,
with Erudites and disciples established to pass on their skills,
the number of musicians reaching over thirty thousand.
6 In the third month,
on Guǐhài day,
the Emperor traveled to the Jiāngdū Palace.
7 Earlier,
the Emperor wished to extensively construct the Fényáng Palace,
and ordered the Censor-in-Chief Zhāng Héng to prepare plans and submit them.
(Textual analysis note: The biography of Zhāng Héng says,
"The year after the Emperor visited Héng's residence,
he traveled to the Fényáng Palace."
It also says,
"The following year,
he again traveled to the Fényáng Palace."
According to the basic annals, none of these events occurred,
so the biography is likely mistaken.)
Héng took the opportunity to advise:
"In recent years, labor services have been numerous,
and the common people are exhausted and impoverished.
I humbly hope Your Majesty will pay attention
and slightly reduce and restrain them."
The Emperor was very displeased.
Later, looking at Héng, he said to his attending ministers:
"Zhāng Héng thinks that because of his planning,
I have obtained the empire."

He then recorded instances such as Prince Qí, Jiǎn, bringing Huángfǔ Xǔ in his retinue, and when he previously traveled to Zhuō Commandery to sacrifice at Héng Mountain, the elders who came to pay their respects were often not properly dressed.
He reprimanded Héng, as the head of the Censorate, for failing to correct such matters.
(Zhāng Héng was the Censor-in-Chief,
hence he was reprimanded for failing in his official duties as head of the Censorate.)
After some time,
Héng supervised the labor of building Lóufán City.
(In the fourth year of the Dàyè era,
Lóufán Commandery was established.
It was the Lán Prefecture of the Later Wèi,
originally the location of Fényáng County of the Hàn.
At that time, the Fényáng Palace was being built,
hence the city was constructed.)
(Shǒu is pronounced with the *shì* and *yòu* fanqie spellings.)
He obtained an audience with the Emperor.
The Emperor disliked that Héng had not become thin and haggard,
considering it a sign that he did not reflect on his fault.
He said to Héng:
"You look quite plump and glossy,
you should return to your commandery for now."
He sent him back to Yùlín.
Not long after,
he ordered Héng to supervise the labor on the Jiāngdū Palace.
When the Minister of Rites Yáng Xuǎngǎn arrived on a mission to Jiāngdū,
Héng said to Xuǎngǎn:
"Xuē Dàohéng truly died unjustly."
Xuǎngǎn reported this;
the Assistant Commandery Governor of Jiāngdū, Wáng Shìchōng, also reported that Héng frequently reduced and skimped on supplies and equipment.
The Emperor then became angry,
had him shackled and brought to the Jiāngdū market,
intending to execute him.
After a long time, he was released,
stripped of his official status and made a commoner,
and sent back to his hometown.
Wáng Shìchōng was put in charge of the Jiāngdū Palace Directorate.
Shìchōng was originally a Hu person from the Western Regions,
surnamed Zhī.
His father, Shōu,
when young, followed his mother in marrying into the Wáng family,
and thus falsely assumed their surname.
Shìchōng was cunning and deceitful by nature,
eloquent in speech,
somewhat versed in books and histories,
fond of military strategy,
and familiar with laws and statutes.
The Emperor frequently visited Jiāngdū,
and Shìchōng was adept at observing his expressions to flatter him,
embellishing ponds and terraces,
and presenting rare treasures,
thereby gaining favor.
This laid the groundwork for Wáng Shìchōng to seize the opportunity and usurp power.
Sì,
pronounced as xiàng lì fān.
8 Summer,
sixth month,
on Jiǎyín,
it was decreed that the rank of the Governor of Jiāngdū be equal to that of the Capital Prefect.
According to Suí regulations,
the Capital Prefect was of the third rank.
9 Winter,
twelfth month,
on Jǐwèi,
Wén'ān Xiàn Hóu Niú Hóng died.
According to Niú Hóng's biography: Hóng held the title of Duke of Qízhāng Commandery,
and upon his death was posthumously granted the title of Marquis of Wén'ān County,
with the posthumous name Xiàn.
This records his posthumous title and name.
Suí records: Wén'ān County belonged to Héjiān Commandery.
Zú,
pronounced as zǐ xù fān.
His scholarship was profound and extensive,
and among the old ministers of the Suí court,
he alone was trusted from beginning to end,
without ever incurring regret or blame.
Only Hóng was such a person.
His younger brother, Bì,
was fond of wine and unruly.
Once, while drunk, he shot and killed the ox pulling Hóng's carriage.
When Hóng returned home,
his wife met him and said:
"Your younger brother shot and killed the ox."
Hóng showed no surprise or inquiry,
but simply replied:
"Make dried meat."
After sitting down,
his wife said again:
"Your younger brother suddenly shot and killed the ox,
which is a very strange matter!"
Hóng said:
"I already know."
His expression remained unchanged,
and he continued reading without pause.
10 An imperial edict ordered the excavation of the Jiāngnán Canal,
from Jīngkǒu to Yúháng,
over eight hundred lǐ long.
This is the present-day canal in Zhèxī, running from Hángzhōu to Zhènjiāng Prefecture and entering the Great River.
Zhènjiāng,
was ancient Jīngkǒu.
The Emperor changed Hángzhōu to Yúháng Commandery.
It was made passable for dragon boats,
and relay stations, palaces, and resting posts were established along it,
intending to tour east to Kuàijī.
The Emperor changed Yuèzhōu back to Kuàijī Commandery.
Kuài,
pronounced as gǔ wài fān.
11 The Emperor, because all officials accompanying the imperial carriage wore kùxí garments,
which were inconvenient during military campaigns,
in this year,
first decreed
"Those accompanying the imperial carriage on distant journeys,
both civil and military officials shall wear military attire.
Those of the fifth rank and above,
shall uniformly wear purple robes;
those of the sixth rank and below,
shall use crimson and green interchangeably.
From then on, the regular attire of civil and military officials
thus became distinguished by rank color.
Zhuó,
pronounced as zé lüè fān.
Fēi,
pronounced as fēi.
Commoners wore white,
butchers and merchants wore black,
soldiers wore yellow."
12 When the Emperor visited Qǐmín's tent,
see the third year of the previous volume.
Qǐmín did not dare to conceal him,
and brought him to see the Emperor.
The Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat, Péi Jǔ, advised the Emperor, saying:
"Gāolì was originally the territory enfeoffed to Jīzǐ;
during the Hàn and Jìn dynasties, it was all commanderies and counties.
King Wǔ of Zhōu enfeoffed Jīzǐ at Cháoxiǎn.
At the end of the Qín, Wèi Mǎn occupied it,
and the state was transmitted to his grandson Yòu Qú.
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn destroyed it,
and opened it as four commanderies.
At the end of the Hàn,
Gōngsūn Dù occupied it,
and the state was transmitted to his grandson Yuān.
Wèi destroyed it,
and until Jìn, it was all commanderies and counties.
The ancestors of Gāolì
originated from Fūyú.
Zhūméng established the state,
named Gāogōulí,
and took Gāo as the clan name.
Since the Wèi and Jìn dynasties,
due to military chaos in the Central Plains,
Gāolì encroached inward,
and annexed the territory of Liáodōng.
Shuō,
pronounced as shū ruì fān.
Cháo,
according to the Hànshū commentary, pronounced as cháo.
It became a separate foreign land.
The late Emperor had long wished to campaign against it,
but Yáng Liàng was unworthy,
and the expedition achieved no success.
The event is recorded in the 178th volume, the eighteenth year of Kāihuáng.
How can we not seize it,
allowing a civilized, cultured region
to become a land of barbarians!
Now their envoy has personally seen Qǐmín's entire state submitting to transformation.
We can take advantage of their fear
to compel them to come to court."
The Emperor followed this advice.
He ordered Niú Hóng to proclaim the decree:
"We, due to Qǐmín's sincere devotion in serving the state,
have personally come to his tent.
Next year, We shall go to Zhuōjùn.
When you return, tell the King of Gāolì:
Do not
harbor doubts or fears.
The rites of preservation and nurturing
shall be like those for Qǐmín.
If he does not come to court,
We shall lead Qǐmín to tour his land."
The King of Gāolì, Yuán, was afraid,
but his tributary rituals were rather deficient.
The Emperor planned to campaign against him;
he levied a tax on the wealthy of the empire to buy military horses,
each horse costing up to one hundred thousand coins;
he inspected weapons and equipment,
demanding they be excellent and new.
If any were substandard or defective,
the envoys would immediately execute [the responsible persons].
1 Spring,
first month,
on Rényín,
Zhēndìng Xiāng Hóu Guō Yǎn died.
He was the Marquis of Zhēndìng County.
According to Suí records,
Héngshān Commandery administered Zhēndìng County.
Zú,
pronounced as zǐ xù fān.
2 Second month,
on Jǐwèi,
the Emperor ascended the Diàotái,
overlooking Yángzǐ Ford,
and held a grand feast for all officials.
On Yǐhài,
the Emperor traveled from Jiāngdū to Zhuōjùn,
aboard the dragon boat,
crossing the river and entering the Yǒngjì Canal.
He also ordered officials from the four departments of Selection, Chancellery, Palace Secretariat, and Censorate to conduct selections and appointments before the boat.
Those undergoing selection numbered over three thousand,
some following the boat on foot for over three thousand lǐ,
without receiving assignments,
suffering from cold, hunger, fatigue, and exhaustion,
resulting in one or two out of ten dying.
3 On the Rénwǔ day,
an edict was issued to campaign against Gāolì.
Yuán Hóngsì, the Commander of Yōuzhōu, was ordered
(Note: The Commander offices of various prefectures had already been abolished in the early years of the Dàyè era;
this text refers to Yuán Hóngsì's previous official position.)
The Emperor changed Láizhōu to Dōnglái Commandery.
Officials and clerks supervised the laborers,
who stood in the water day and night,
scarcely daring to rest.
From the waist down, their bodies were infested with maggots,
and three or four out of ten died.
In summer,
the fourth month,
on the Gēngwǔ day,
the imperial carriage arrived at Línshuò Palace in Zhuō Commandery.
(Note: According to the Táng records, Jì County in Yōuzhōu had the former Suí-era Línshuò Palace.)
The Examination of Discrepancies states:
"On the Bǐngwǔ day,
[the Emperor] visited the new palace in Zhuō Commandery."
According to the perpetual calendar,
the first day of this month was Bǐngchén,
so there was no Bǐngwǔ day.
We now follow the Imperial Annals.
[The Emperor] also ordered that residences be provided for their accommodation.
Previously,
an edict had been issued to conscript soldiers from across the realm,
regardless of distance,
all to assemble at Zhuō.
Zhuō
refers to Zhuō Commandery.
(Note: The character "先" is pronounced "xiān.")
(Note: The character "先" is pronounced "xiān.")
Thirty thousand crossbowmen
and thirty thousand shield-bearers from Lǐngnán
were conscripted, and from all directions, people rushed to assemble like flowing water.
In the fifth month,
an order was issued for Hénán, Huáinán, and Jiāngnán to construct fifty thousand military chariots and send them to Gāoyáng.
(Note: According to the Suí records, Gāoyáng County
belonged to Héjiān Commandery.)
(Note: The character "乘" is pronounced "shèng.")
(Note: The character "乘" is pronounced "shèng.")
Soldiers were ordered to pull the chariots themselves,
and laborers from north and south of the Yellow River were conscripted to supply military needs.
In autumn,
the seventh month,
laborers and boats from south of the Jiāng and Huái rivers were mobilized to transport grain from the Líyáng and Luòkǒu granaries to Zhuō Commandery.
Boats stretched in an unbroken line for over a thousand lǐ,
carrying weapons, armor, and equipment for attack and capture.
Tens of thousands of people were constantly on the roads, coming and going,
clogging the routes,
with no respite day or night.
The dead lay piled upon one another,
and the stench of decay filled the roads.
The realm was thrown into turmoil.
4 Floods struck Shāndōng and Hénán,
submerging over thirty commanderies.
In winter,
the tenth month,
on the Yǐmǎo day,
Dǐzhù collapsed,
causing the river to reverse its flow for several dozen lǐ.
(Note: Dǐzhù is located in the river north of Shǎn County in Hénán Commandery.)
(Note: Dǐzhù is located in the river north of Shǎn County in Hénán Commandery.)
(Note: The character "底" is the same as "砥.")
(Note: The character "底" is the same as "砥.")
5 Earlier,
when the Emperor toured the west,
(see the fifth year).
According to Suí regulations: The Censorate had eight Attendant Censors.
[The Emperor] ordered [the Tǔjué] to meet the imperial carriage at Dàdǒubá Gǔ,
but the Tǔjué people did not comply.
Chǔluó apologized to the envoy,
making excuses.
The Emperor was furious,
but could do nothing about it.
At that time, the chieftain Shèkuì sent an envoy to seek a marriage alliance.
Péi Jǔ thus memorialized:
"Chǔluó does not come to court
because he relies on his strength.
I request to use a stratagem to weaken him,
splitting his state,
so that he will be easier to control.
Shèkuì
is the son of Dūliù
and grandson of Dátóu.
(Note: Dù Yòu said: Dūliù was the one who first established the title for the Tūjué.)
(Note: Dù Yòu said: Dūliù was the one who first established the title for the Tūjué.)
Now Jǔ says Dūliù was the son of Dátóu,
so he was not the one who first established the title.)
He rules over the western region.
Now, hearing that he has lost his position
and become subordinate to Chǔluó,
he has sent an envoy to seek support.
I hope to treat his envoy generously,
appoint him as Great Kèhán,
so the Tūjué power will be divided,
and both will submit to us."
(Meaning Shèkuì and Chǔluó will both submit to Suí.)
"Your words are correct."
Thus, [the Emperor] sent Péi Jǔ to the guesthouse morning and evening,
subtly hinting and persuading [the envoy].
The Emperor summoned the envoy at Rénfēng Hall,
spoke of Chǔluó's disobedience,
praised Shèkuì's good intentions,
and said he would appoint him as Great Kèhán,
ordering him to raise troops to attack Chǔluó,
after which a marriage alliance would be made.
The Emperor took a peach-bamboo white-feathered arrow
(Note: Peach bamboo is a type of bamboo.
(Note: Peach bamboo is a type of bamboo.)
It is found in Jiāngnán today.)
and said to him:
"This matter must be swift,
as fast as an arrow."
The envoy returned,
passing through Chǔluó's territory.
Chǔluó admired the arrow
and wanted to keep it,
but the envoy used deception and escaped.
Shèkuì was overjoyed upon hearing this,
raised troops, and attacked Chǔluó.
Chǔluó was badly defeated,
abandoned his wife and children,
and fled east with several thousand cavalry.
Along the way, he was robbed,
took refuge in Gāochāng,
and defended himself east at Shíluómàn Mountain.
(Note: According to the New Táng records, Yīwú County in Yīzhōu has Zhéluómàn Mountain,
also called Tiānshān.)
(Note: The character "將" is pronounced "jiàng,"
(Note: The character "將" is pronounced "jiàng,")
also pronounced as in its original reading,
meaning to lead.)
(Note: The character "騎" is pronounced "jì.")
(Note: The character "騎" is pronounced "jì.")
(Note: The character "被" is pronounced "pī.")
(Note: The character "被" is pronounced "pī.")
[Chǔluó] reported the situation to the Emperor.
(Note: According to the New Táng records, Yùmén Pass is northwest of Shòuchāng County in Shāzhōu.)
In the twelfth month,
on the Jǐwèi day,
Chǔluó came to court at Línshuò Palace.
The Emperor was greatly pleased
and received him with exceptional courtesy.
The Emperor feasted with Chǔluó,
and Chǔluó kowtowed,
apologizing for his late audience.
The Emperor consoled him with kind words,
prepared the finest delicacies from across the realm,
displayed lavish female entertainments,
with silks, music,
dazzling to the eyes and ears.
However, Chǔluó still wore a discontented expression.
6 Since last year, the Emperor had planned to campaign against Gāolì.
He issued an edict to establish offices in Shāndōng,
ordering the rearing of horses for military service.
Laborers were also conscripted to transport grain,
storing it at the two garrisons of Lúhé and Huáiyuǎn.
(Note: According to the New Táng records, during the Suí era, Liáoxī Commandery was established at the old city of Rǔluó in Yíngzhōu,
(Note: According to the New Táng records, during the Suí era, Liáoxī Commandery was established at the old city of Rǔluó in Yíngzhōu,)
governing Liáoxī, Lúhé, and Huáiyuǎn counties.)
(Note: The character "瀘" is pronounced "lú.")
(Note: The character "瀘" is pronounced "lú.")
More than half of the soldiers died,
farming missed its season,
and many fields were left fallow.
Famine was added to this,
grain prices soared,
especially in the northeastern border regions,
where a dǒu of rice cost several hundred coins.
Some of the transported grain was coarse and spoiled,
but the people were ordered to buy it and pay compensation.
Moreover, over six hundred thousand handcart laborers were conscripted.
(Note: Handcarts are small carts,
(Note: Handcarts are small carts,)
said to be so small they can only hold a deer.)
The roads were dangerous and distant,
and the rations were insufficient.
Upon reaching the garrisons,
they had nothing to deliver,
and all feared punishment and became fugitives.
Moreover, officials were greedy and cruel,
exploiting and plundering along the way.
The people were impoverished,
their resources and strength exhausted.
If they remained peacefully, they could not endure the cold and hunger;
death pressed upon them urgently.

Shǎo
is pronounced shī zhǎo fān.
Fúwēi had Gōngshí station troops strictly outside,
while he himself, with about ten attendants, brought cattle and wine to pay his respects at Pòchén's seat,
killed Pòchén,
and absorbed his followers.
The history states that Dù Fúwēi gradually grew stronger.
1 Spring,
Kǎoyì says: Zájì records:
"In the first month of this year,
Yǔwén Shù, the Duke of Xǔ, was again appointed Marshal,
leading 160,000 troops, scheduled to reach the Yālǜ River.
Yīzhī Wéndé sent an envoy pretending to surrender to delay our army,
and requested to meet with Shù,
to observe the situation of our army.
Shù drank happily with him,
and after a long time, he left.
After stopping for five days,
our army's provisions were exhausted.
They burned armor and ate it,
and the soldiers fell ill and could not rise.
Wéndé then unleashed his troops for a great battle.
Our army was defeated,
with over 100,000 dead."
This probably describes events of the 8th year,
mistakenly placed here.
On Xīnwèi,
the Emperor ordered all officials to discuss attacking Gāolì.
For several days,
no one dared to speak.
On Wùzǐ,
the Emperor issued an edict to again conscript troops from across the empire,
advancing in a hundred columns.
2 On Dīngyǒu,
the bandit leader Táng Bì of Fúfēng established Lǐ Hóngzhī as Son of Heaven,
with a following of 100,000,
and called himself King of Táng.
3 In the third month,
on Rénzǐ,
the Emperor traveled to Zhuō Commandery.
Soldiers on the road
deserted one after another.
On Guǐhài,
he reached the Línyú Palace.
According to the Suí dynasty records: Lúlóng County in Běipíng Commandery had the Línyú Palace.
Yú
is pronounced yù,
also pronounced yú.
Zhèng Xuán said: Mà
is a military sacrifice,
performed in the field, it is called mà.
Yīng Shào said: The Yellow Emperor fought at Bǎnquán to stabilize the world,
so this sacrifice is performed to seek blessings and good fortune.
Dù Yòu said: Mà
is a military sacrifice,
a prayer for the army.
The deity is probably Chīyóu,
or some say the Yellow Emperor.
According to the system of the Northern Qí,
when the Son of Heaven personally led a campaign,
as he approached the battlefield,
a hard day was chosen by divination.
Black sacrificial animals were prepared,
the army's formation was displayed,
and an altar was set up in the chén direction.
A shàn altar was made for the mà sacrifice.
The Grand Minister of War presented arrows,
the officials presented hair and blood,
music played the Dà Huò melody,
and after the rites, the sacrificial animals were removed and burned.
According to the record in Wángzhì,
when the Son of Heaven went on an expedition,
he performed the mà sacrifice at the place of the expedition.
That ritual is now lost.
What Dù Yòu recorded
is the ritual of the Northern Qí.
Mà
is pronounced mǎ jià fān.
They beheaded a man and smeared his blood on the drums.
4 Summer,
fourth month,
the Tàishǒu of Yúlín, Chéngjì's Dǒng Chún
The Emperor changed Shèngzhōu to Yúlín Commandery.
According to the Suí dynasty records,
Chéngjì County belonged to Tiānshuǐ Commandery.
Shǒu
is pronounced shì yòu fān.
The Emperor changed Xúzhōu to Péngchéng Commandery.
Chānglǜ
was a Hàn dynasty county,
recorded in the histories of Jìn, Sòng, and Wèi.
It had been abolished by the Suí dynasty,
and its territory likely fell within the boundaries of Lánlíng County in Péngchéng Commandery.
Shuài
is pronounced suǒ lèi fān;
same below.
Lǜ
is pronounced lú.
They beheaded over 10,000.
5 On Jiǎwǔ,
the imperial carriage reached Běipíng.
The Emperor changed Píngzhōu to Běipíng Commandery.
6 In the fifth month, on the Gēngshēn day,
the rebel leader Liú Jiālùn of Yán'ān
(Sui Records: Yán'ān Commandery was established as Dōngxià Province during the Later Wei,
renamed Yán Province during the Western Wei,
and the Emperor changed it to Yán'ān Commandery.)
(Jiā is pronounced jiā.)
Textual Analysis says: The Book of Tang records him as "a man of Āndìng."
According to this, Āndìng is too far from Shàngjùn,
so we follow the Book of Sui.
He established the era name Dàshì,
had a following of one hundred thousand,
and collaborated with the Jīhú people in raiding.
An edict appointed General of the Left Xiaowei Qūtū Tōng as the Grand Commissioner for Pacification within the Passes,
and troops were dispatched to attack him.
They fought at Shàngjùn.
(Sui Records: Shàngjùn was established as Dōngqín Province during the Later Wei,
later renamed Běihuá Province,
renamed Fū Province during the Western Wei,
renamed Fūchéng Commandery in the second year of the Daye era,
and later renamed Shàngjùn.)
(Xiāo is pronounced jiān yáo.
Qū is pronounced jū wù.
Shǐ is pronounced shū lì.
Fū is pronounced fū.)
Tens of thousands of men and women were captured and taken back.
7 In autumn, in the seventh month, on the Guǐchǒu day,
the imperial carriage halted at Huáiyuǎn Garrison.
At that time, the empire was already in chaos;
many of the conscripted troops failed to arrive on time,
and Gāogōulì was also exhausted and weakened.
Lái Hù'ér reached Bìshē City (which is Bēishā City).
(From the sea route via Dēng and Lái heading toward Píngrǎng, one first reaches Bēishā City.
In the late Zhēnguàn era of the Tang, Chéng Míngzhèn also took this route.)
(Lì is pronounced lì zhī.)
Lái Hù'ér attacked and defeated them,
and was about to advance toward Píngrǎng.
Gāoyuán, the king of Gāogōulì, became fearful.
On the Jiǎzǐ day,
he sent an envoy to beg for surrender,
and sent Húsī Zhèng, held captive, as an offering.
(Húsī Zhèng had fled to Gāogōulì the previous year.)
(Shǐ is pronounced shū lì; the same below.)
(Xiáng is pronounced hù jiāng.)
An envoy bearing the imperial tally was sent to summon Lái Hù'ér to return.
Lái Hù'ér gathered his troops and said:
"The grand army has gone out three times,
yet we have not been able to pacify the enemy.
If we return this time, we cannot come again;
to toil without achieving merit—I privately feel ashamed.
Now Gāogōulì is truly exhausted;
with these troops attacking them,
we can conquer them in a matter of days.
I wish to advance and directly besiege Píngrǎng,
capture Gāoyuán,
and return after presenting victory—would that not be excellent?"
He submitted a memorial requesting to proceed,
refusing to obey the edict.
Chief Clerk Cuī Jūnsù firmly argued against it,
but Lái Hù'ér would not relent,
saying:
"The enemy's strength is already broken;
with me solely in command,
it is sufficient to handle it.
I am outside the capital;
matters should be decided independently.
I would rather capture Gāoyuán and return to face reprimand
than abandon this chance of success—that I cannot do!"
Cuī Jūnsù announced to the troops:
"If you follow the commander-in-chief in disobeying and resisting the imperial edict,
it will certainly be reported to the throne,
and all will be held guilty."
The various generals became fearful
and all requested to return;
only then did he obey the edict.
In the eighth month, on the Jǐsì day,
the Emperor set out on the return journey from Huáiyuǎn Garrison.
The rebel leader Yáng Gōngqīng of Hándān led his faction of eight thousand men
(Sui Records: Hándān County belonged to Wǔ'ān Commandery.)
(Shuài is pronounced shuài.)
and seized forty-two imperial horses of the Feihuáng breed before departing.
In winter, in the tenth month, on the Dīngmǎo day,
the Emperor arrived at the Eastern Capital;
on the Jǐchǒu day,
he returned to the Western Capital.
He used the Gāogōulì envoy and Húsī Zhèng to report to the Imperial Ancestral Temple;
he still summoned King Gāoyuán of Gāogōulì to court,
but Gāoyuán ultimately did not come.
An order was issued for the generals to prepare strictly,
planning another campaign later,
but it ultimately did not materialize.
Earlier, at the end of the Kāihuáng era,
the state was prosperous and flourishing,
and both court and commoners were intent on Gāogōulì.
Only Liú Xuàn considered it inadvisable,
composing the "Essay on Pacifying the Barbarians" to criticize it.
By this time,
his words began to prove true.
In the eleventh month, on the Bǐngshēn day,
Húsī Zhèng was executed outside the Jīnguāng Gate.
(Jīnguāng Gate was the central gate among the three gates on the west side of Dàxīng City.)
(The previous year, Yáng Jīshàn was executed.)
Officials were made to eat his flesh;
flatterers ate until they were full.
The remaining bones were collected,
burned, and scattered.
8 On the Yǐsì day,
a ceremony was held at the southern suburb altar.
The Emperor did not fast in the preparatory chamber.
(Zheng Xuan said: The preparatory chamber is the place for self-cultivation and purification.)
The imperial carriage with full ceremonial trappings was prepared.
(The Han followed the Qin system: the Grand Procession had eighty-one carriages, the Ceremonial Procession thirty-six.
During the Sui Kāihuáng era, the Grand Procession had twelve carriages, the Ceremonial Procession half that.
The Emperor revised the system: the Grand Procession used thirty-six, the Ceremonial Procession used twelve.)
(Qià is pronounced qù jí.)
On that day,
there was a great wind.
The Emperor alone made offerings to the Supreme Deity,
while the Three Dukes separately made offerings to the Five Deities.
After the rites were completed,
he mounted his horse and galloped swiftly back.
9 On the Yǐmǎo day,
the Hú rebel Liú Miáowáng of Líshí rebelled.
(Sui Records: Líshí Commandery was established as Xīfén Province during the Later Qi,
renamed Fén Province during the Later Zhou,
and the Emperor changed it to Líshí Commandery.)
His followers numbered tens of thousands.
General Pān Chángwén was sent to suppress him,
but was unsuccessful.
10 The rebel leader Wáng Dérén of Jí Commandery gathered a following of tens of thousands,
holding Línlǜ Mountain as a stronghold for banditry.
(Sui Records: Jí Commandery was established as Yì Province during the Eastern Wei,
renamed Wèi Province during the Later Zhou,
and the Emperor changed it to Jí Commandery.
Línlǜ Mountain is in Línlǜ County of Wèi Commandery.)
(Shuài is pronounced suǒ lèi; the same below.)
(Lǜ is pronounced lú.)
11. The emperor was about to travel to the Eastern Capital.
The Grand Astrologer Yǔ Zhì remonstrated, saying:
"In recent years, campaigns have been waged against Liáo,
and the people are truly weary and exhausted.
Your Majesty should pacify and govern the Guānzhōng region,
enabling the common people to devote their efforts to agriculture and sericulture.
Within three to five years,
when the realm is somewhat prosperous and well-supplied,
then undertaking an imperial tour and inspection
would be appropriate for the affairs of state."
The emperor was displeased.
Yǔ Zhì pleaded illness and did not accompany him.
The emperor grew angry,
imprisoned Yǔ Zhì,
and he ultimately died in prison.
In the twelfth month,
on the Rénshēn day,
the emperor traveled to the Eastern Capital,
granting a general amnesty to the realm.
On the Wùzǐ day,
he entered the Eastern Capital.
12. The bandit leader Péng Xiàocái from Dōnghǎi moved around plundering Yíshuǐ.
Liú Xù said: Yíshuǐ
was the Dōngguǎn County of the Hàn dynasty.
In the Suí dynasty, it was renamed Dōng'ān County,
and soon after changed to Yíshuǐ,
belonging to Lángyá Commandery.
Although Dǒng Chún achieved frequent victories in battle,
bandits and rebels increased daily.
Someone slandered Dǒng Chún as timid and cowardly.
The emperor grew angry,
had Dǒng Chún shackled and sent to the Eastern Capital,
and executed him.
13. Mèng Ràng, from Chángbáishān, raided and plundered various commanderies,
reaching Xūyí,
with a force of over one hundred thousand men.
He occupied the Dūliáng Palace.
The Suí Records state: Xūyí County belonged to Jiāngdū Commandery,
and there was Dūliáng Mountain.
The Dūliáng Palace was located there.
The mountain produced dūliáng incense,
hence the name.
Xūyí
is pronounced xū yí.
Wáng Shìchōng, the Assistant Magistrate of Jiāngdū, led troops to resist him,
constructing five stockades to block the strategic passes,
feigning weakness by displaying a meager appearance.
Mèng Ràng laughed and said:
"Wáng Shìchōng is a petty clerk versed in administrative procedures;
how could he command troops!
I will capture him alive now,
and march triumphantly into Jiāngdū!"
At that time, the people had all built fortresses to protect themselves,
so there was nothing to plunder in the countryside.
The bandit forces gradually grew hungry.
Therefore, Mèng Ràng left a small force
to besiege the five stockades,
and divided his men to plunder in the southern regions.
Wáng Shìchōng, waiting for their moment of laxity,
unleashed his troops in an attack,
routing them decisively.
Mèng Ràng fled with several dozen cavalry,
and over ten thousand heads were taken.
14. The bandit leader Zuǒ Xiàoyǒu from Qí Commandery, with a force of one hundred thousand men, camped at Dūngǒu Mountain.
"Dūngǒu"
derives its name from its shape.
Dūn
is pronounced cún.
Zuǒ Xiàoyǒu, hard-pressed, came out and surrendered.
Zhāng Xūntuó's might shook the eastern region.
For his achievements, he was promoted to Tōngshǒu of Qí Commandery.
The emperor abolished provinces and established commanderies,
with each commandery having a Tàishǒu.
Afterwards, each commandery additionally established one Tōngshǒu,
whose rank was below the Tàishǒu.
Shǒu
is pronounced shòu.
The bandit leader Lú Míngyuè from Zhuō Commandery, with a force of over one hundred thousand men, encamped at Zhù'ā.
The Suí Records state: Zhù'ā County
belonged to Qí Commandery.
In the Táng dynasty, it was renamed Yǔchéng County.
Examination of discrepancies: The Táng biography of Qín Shūbǎo says
"Xiàpī".
Here we follow the Suí Shū.
They faced each other for over ten days.
When provisions were exhausted,
and they were about to retreat,
Zhāng Xūntuó said to his officers and men:
"When the bandits see us retreat,
they will certainly pursue with their entire force.
If a thousand men could launch a surprise attack and seize their camp,
there could be great advantage.
This is truly a dangerous undertaking;
who is willing to go?"
No one among the multitude responded,
only Luó Shìxìn and Qín Shūbǎo from Lìchéng requested to go.
The Suí Records state: Lìchéng County was attached to Qí Commandery.
He sent the two men, each leading a thousand soldiers, to lie in ambush among the reeds.
Lú Míngyuè pursued with his entire force.
Luó Shìxìn and Qín Shūbǎo galloped to his stockade.
The stockade gate was closed.
The two men scaled and ascended its tower,
each killing several men,
causing great chaos in the camp.
The two men broke open the gate to admit the external troops,
then set fire, burning over thirty of his stockades.
Smoke and flames billowed to the sky.
Lú Míngyuè fled back.
Zhāng Xūntuó turned his army around and attacked fiercely,
routing him decisively.
Lú Míngyuè escaped with several hundred cavalry.
The number of captives and beheaded was incalculable.
Qín Shūbǎo's given name was Qióng,
but he was known by his courtesy name.
1. In spring,
the first month,
one hundred and twenty additional officials were added to the Imperial Library Directorate.
According to Suí regulations: The Imperial Library Directorate
had one Director and one Assistant Director each,
four Gentlemen,
twelve Editorial Assistants,
four Textual Critics,
two Historiographers,
eight Assistant Historiographers,
and two each of Editorial Assistants and Textual Critics.
The emperor added one Vice Director,
reduced the Editorial Assistants to ten,
and added four Assistant Historiographers.
He also established ten Scholars of Confucian Learning,
twenty Scholars of Literary Arts,
increased the number of Editorial Assistants by forty,
and added twenty Scribes,
totaling one hundred and seventeen persons.
The emperor was fond of reading books and composing writings.
Since he became the Governor-General of Yángzhōu,
in the tenth year of the Kāihuáng era,
the emperor was Governor-General of Yángzhōu.
Fond
is pronounced hào.
He constantly ordered compilations and writings,
and upon becoming emperor,
for nearly twenty years in total,
compilation and writing never ceased for a moment.
From the classics and scholarship, literature, military affairs, agriculture, geography, medicine, divination, Buddhism, Daoism, down to gambling, falconry, and dogs,
all were made into new books,
none not meticulously comprehensive,
altogether completing thirty-one sections,
over seventeen thousand scrolls.
Initially,
the Jiāzé Hall of the Western Capital held three hundred and seventy thousand scrolls of books.
The emperor ordered the Imperial Library Director Liǔ Gùyán and others to collate and arrange them,
removing duplicates and miscellaneous works,
obtaining over thirty-seven thousand scrolls of the orthodox imperial collection,
which were stored in the Xiūwén Hall of the Eastern Capital.
Furthermore, fifty duplicate copies were made,
categorized into three grades,
and distributed to the palaces, directorates, and government offices of the Western and Eastern Capitals.
The main
books were all bound beautifully and cleanly,
with precious rollers and brocade covers.
In front of the Guānwén Hall, fourteen library rooms were built.
The windows, doors, beds, mattresses, cabinets, and curtains
were all extremely luxurious and splendid.
Every three rooms formed a square space,
with brocade curtains hanging in the doorways.
Above were two flying immortals.
Outside the doorway on the ground, mechanisms were installed.
When the emperor visited the library,
palace attendants holding incense burners,
incense burners originated in the Hàn.
The Hàn Official Duties states: The Gentleman of the Imperial Secretariat was provided with two female scribes,
dressed in clean clothes,
holding incense burners for fumigation.
then the flying immortals would descend,
retract the curtains and ascend,
the door leaves and cabinet doors would all open automatically.
When the emperor left,
they would close and return to their former state.
2. Because households were fleeing and absconding,
and bandits and rebels were numerous,
in the second month,
on the Gēngwǔ day,
an edict was issued ordering the people all to reside within walled cities,
with farmland allocated nearby.
The post stations, relay stations, villages, and forts of the commanderies and counties were all to build walls.
3. The bandit leader Wáng Xūbá from Shànggǔ proclaimed himself the Carefree Heavenly King,
with the state name Yān.
The bandit leader Wèi Dāo'ér proclaimed himself Lìshānfēi. Each had a force of over one hundred thousand men,
allying with the Tūjué in the north,
and raiding Yān and Zhào in the south.
4. Initially,
Emperor Gaozu dreamed that floodwaters submerged the capital city,
which he found ominous,
so he moved the capital to Dàxīng.
In the third year of the Kāihuáng era,
he relocated to the new capital.
The death of Mù is recorded in volume 176, under the fourth year of the Zhìdé era of Chén Chángchénggōng.
His uncle Hún resented his stinginess,
and had his elder brother's son Shànhéng murder him,
then framed his paternal cousin Qútán,
causing him to be executed in compensation.
Hún said to his wife's elder brother, Left Guard Commander Yǔwén Shù:
"If I can inherit the title,
I will offer half of the state's annual tax revenue to you."
Shù spoke on his behalf to the Crown Prince,
who petitioned Emperor Gaozu,
and Hún was made Mù's heir.
Two years later,
he no longer gave the state tax revenue to Shù,
and Shù deeply resented him.
When Emperor Yáng ascended the throne,
Hún rose through the ranks to become General of the Right Valiant Guard,
and was enfeoffed as Duke of Chéng.
The Emperor, wary of his powerful clan,
grew suspicious of him.
At that time, a fāngshì named Ān Jiātuó
claimed
"the Lǐ family will become the Son of Heaven,"
and urged the Emperor to exterminate everyone in the land surnamed Lǐ.
Hún's nephew, the Director of the Palace Buildings, Mǐn,
whose childhood name was Hóng'ér,
made the Emperor suspect that his name corresponded to the prophecy,
so the Emperor often told him to his face,
hoping he would take his own life.
Mǐn was greatly frightened,
and frequently whispered privately with Hún and Shànhéng, dismissing others;
Shù slandered them to the Emperor,
and also sent the Tiger Guard General Péi Rénjī of Hédōng to submit a memorial accusing Hún of rebellion.
The Emperor changed Púzhōu to Hédōng Commandery.
Bēn,
pronounced bēn.
Jiàng,
pronounced jí liàng fān;
same below.
He sent the Left Assistant of the Department of State Affairs Yuán Wéndōu and the Censor-in-Chief Péi Yùn to jointly investigate the case,
but after several days of interrogation,
they found no evidence of rebellion,
and reported the truth to the Emperor.
The Emperor then sent Shù to investigate exhaustively,
and Shù induced Mǐn's wife, Lady Yǔwén, to write a memorial,
falsely accusing Hún of plotting to take advantage of the campaign against Liáodōng,
join forces with members of his clan who were generals,
and attack the imperial camp to establish Mǐn as the Son of Heaven.
Shù took the memorial
and presented it to the Emperor,
who wept and said:
"My ancestral temple was nearly overturned,
but thanks to you, it has been preserved."
In the third month,
on the day Dīngyǒu,
Hún, Mǐn, Shànhéng, and thirty-two members of their clan were executed,
and all relatives within the third degree of mourning were exiled to the borderlands.
Several months later,
Mǐn's wife was also poisoned to death.
Mǐn's wife, Lady Yǔwén,
was the daughter of Zhōu Tiānyuán,
and the Emperor's niece.
5. Two peacocks flew from the Western Park and gathered in front of the audience hall in Bǎochéng.
The Western Park was west of Luòchéng,
built in the first year.
Later, when Táng troops attacked Wáng Shìchōng,
Shìchōng had his younger brother Shìwěi guard Bǎochéng,
indicating that Bǎochéng was within the outer walls of Luòchéng,
forming its own city.
Since the audience hall was located there,
the offices of all government departments were also there,
making it a separate city,
attached to the southeast of the palace city.
The Táng dynasty followed the Sui system,
also making Luòyáng the Eastern Capital.
The Liù Diǎn states: the Eastern City is east of the Imperial City,
the Imperial City is within the Eastern City,
the offices of all officials follow the system of the capital,
and the imperial palace is north of the Imperial City.
From this, I deduce
that the Imperial City was likely the Sui's Bǎochéng,
located southeast of the palace city.
Cháo,
pronounced zhí yáo fān;
same below.
Mǎ Dérú reported them as luán birds,
and the Emperor established the Personal Attendant Yīngyáng Prefecture,
overseeing the Personal, Meritorious, and Martial Attendants.
The three attendants,
namely the three guards,
each had a Commandant of the Rapid Cavalry and a Commandant of the Infantry.
Examination of discrepancies: the Zá Jì states:
"In the second month of the fifth year,
Mǎ Dérú reported peacocks as luán birds."
The year, month, and surname here follow the Lüè Jì and Wēn Dàyǎ's Chuàngyè Qǐjū Zhù.
With no way to verify,
all officials offered congratulations.
An edict praised Dérú for his sincere heart and profound insight,
being the first to witness this auspicious sign,
promoted him to Court Gentleman for Consultation,
awarded him one hundred bolts of silk,
and gave bundles of silk to others;
and also ordered the construction of the Yìluán Hall at that location.
6. On the day Jǐyǒu,
the Emperor traveled to Tàiyuán;
in summer,
the fourth month,
he went to the Fényáng Palace to escape the heat.
The palace city was cramped,
so officials and soldiers scattered among the valleys,
building thatched huts to live in.
7. Lǐ Yuān, the Junior Minister of the Court of the Imperial Guard, was appointed as the Grand Commissioner of Pacification and Comfort for Shānxī and Hédōng,
authorized to promote, demote, select, and appoint civil and military officials in the commanderies and counties,
and to mobilize troops from Hédōng to suppress bandits.
Yuān traveled to Lóngmén,
attacked the bandit leader Wú Duān'ér,
and defeated him.
Liú Xù said: Lóngmén,
was the Hàn dynasty's Àishì County,
renamed Lóngmén by the Later Wèi;
the Sui records place it in Hédōng Commandery.
Shuài,
pronounced suǒ lèi fān.
Wú,
pronounced wú,
is a surname.
8. In autumn,
the eighth month,
on the day Yǐchǒu,
the Emperor toured the northern frontier.
Examination of discrepancies: the Zá Jì states:
"In the sixth month,
Turkic bandits raided Lánchéng Town,
Fàn Ānguì was sent to attack them,
but the imperial army was defeated,
Ānguì died,
and all officials were terrified.
In the seventh month,
the Emperor went to Yànmén,
first arriving at Tiānchí,
where it rained,
the mud in the valleys was two feet deep,
the accompanying officials were in disarray,
most tents did not arrive,
they spent the night sitting in the rain,
and many died by dawn,
the palace attendants had no food,
and borrowed dried provisions from the guards."
Here, the Suí Shū is followed.
Initially,
Péi Jǔ, seeing that the tribe of the Turkic Shǐbì Kèhán was growing stronger,
proposed a strategy to divide their power,
intending to marry a imperial clan daughter to his younger brother Chìjíshè,
and appoint him as the Southern Kèhán;
Chìjí did not dare accept,
and Shǐbì gradually grew resentful upon hearing of it.
The Turkic minister Shǐshǔ Húxī, who was resourceful and strategic,
was favored and trusted by Shǐbì.
Jǔ pretended to engage in trade with him,
lured him to beneath Mǎyì,
and killed him.
The Emperor changed Shuòzhōu to Mǎyì Commandery.
Yòu,
pronounced yǒu.
"Shǐshǔ Húxī betrayed the Kèhán and came to surrender,
and I have already executed him on your behalf."

detain their leaders,
and alone escort Duke Liáng to seize the commandery city,
then no one will be above me."
So he killed Déjī.
Entering to report to Xiǎn,
Xiǎn was greatly shocked and said:
"Now we wish to bring order from chaos,
yet suddenly kill each other,
I cannot be your leader."
Then walked out of the army gate.
Liǔshēng was greatly afraid,
prostrated to beg for forgiveness,
Xiǎn reprimanded but pardoned him,
arrayed troops and entered the city.
Jǐngzhēn said to Xiǎn:
"Xú Déjī was a meritorious official of the righteous uprising,
yet Liǔshēng killed him without reason,
if this is not punished,
how can we govern!
Moreover, Liǔshēng has long been a bandit,
though now he follows righteousness,
his violent nature remains unchanged,
sharing one city,
he will surely cause trouble.
If we miss this chance,
regret will be too late!"
Xiǎn again agreed.
Jǐngzhēn arrested Liǔshēng,
executed him,
his followers all fled.
On the bǐngshēn day,
Xiǎn built an altar and lit a fire sacrifice,
proclaimed himself King of Liáng,
changed the era name to Míngfèng.
18 On the rényín day,
Wáng Shìchōng crossed the Luò River at night,
encamped at Hēishí,
the next day,
divided troops to guard the camp,
personally led elite troops to array north of the Luò.
Lǐ Mì heard of this,
led troops across the Luò to engage in battle,
Mì's troops were greatly defeated,
Chái Xiàohé drowned.
Mì led his elite cavalry across the Luò to the south,
the remaining forces fled east to Yuèchéng,
Yuèchéng,
likely a crescent-shaped city built near the Luò River,
corresponding to the granary city.
Mì rode from south of the Luò straight toward Hēishí,
the camp was frightened,
lit six beacon fires in succession,
Shìchōng lifted the siege of Yuèchéng,
hurriedly returned to rescue;
Mì turned back to engage in battle,
greatly defeated them,
beheading over three thousand.
On the 19th day, the jia-chén day,
Lǐ Yuān ordered his armies to attack the city,
stipulating that
"No one is to violate the seven ancestral temples or the imperial clan of the Prince of Dài.
Violators will have their three clans exterminated!"
Sūn Huá died after being struck by a stray arrow.
In the eleventh month,
on the bǐng-chén day,
the army commander Léi Yǒngjí was the first to ascend the walls.
A note on discrepancies: The "Veritable Records of Emperor Gaozu of Táng" records
"Léi Shào".
We now follow the "Annotations on the Founding".
The Prince of Dài was in the Eastern Palace.
His attendants had all fled and scattered,
with only the Reader-in-Waiting Yáo Sīlián remaining by his side.
When the soldiers were about to ascend the hall,
Sīlián sternly rebuked them, saying:
"The Duke of Táng has raised a righteous army to uphold the imperial house.
How dare you show such disrespect!"
The crowd was taken aback,
and they stood arrayed in the courtyard below.
Yuān received the Prince at the Eastern Palace
and moved him to reside behind the Dàxīng Hall.
The Dàxīng Hall
was the main hall of the Suí palace.
As he had not yet assumed the imperial position,
he therefore resided behind the hall.
[Yuān] wept, bowed, and departed.
Sīlián
was the son of Yáo Chá.
Yáo Chá
served the Chén dynasty
and was renowned for his literary talent and righteousness.
[Lǐ Yuān] took up residence in the Chánglè Palace,
established a twelve-article covenant with the people,
and abolished all the harsh prohibitions of Suí.

Zhai Rang's Marshal, Wáng Rúxìn, advised Rang to appoint himself as Grand Steward,
overseeing all affairs,
in order to seize Mì's authority.
Rang did not comply.
Rang's elder brother, Pillar of State and Duke of Xíngyáng, Hóng,
(Textual Analysis says: Héluò Jì writes
"Hóng."
Now following the Biography of the Duke of Púshān.)
said to Rang:
"The Son of Heaven, you should be it yourself,
why give it to another!
If you won't do it,
I will!"
Rang merely laughed heartily,
not taking it seriously.
Mì heard of this and was displeased.
Commander Cuī Shìshū, newly attached to Mì from Yānlíng,
(Yānlíng County,
belonged to Yǐngchuān Commandery during Sui.)
(Yān,
read as yèwǎn,
also yújiàn,
also pronounced yǎn.)
was demanded for goods.
Shìshū had not yet managed to procure them,
and they hastily wanted to punish him.
Rang summoned the Marshal's Office Registrar, Xíng Yìqī, to gamble,
but he hesitated and did not come promptly,
so they caned him eighty strokes.
Rang said to Left Chief of Staff Fáng Yànzǎo:
"You previously captured Rǔnán,
obtaining much treasure and goods,
yet you gave it all to Duke Wèi,
and gave me none at all!
Duke Wèi was established by me;
how things will turn out is uncertain!"
Yànzǎo became afraid,
and reported the situation to Mì,
then together with Left Marshal Zhèng Tǐng, they advised Mì, saying:
"Rang is greedy, obstinate, and unkind,
harboring disloyal thoughts towards his lord.
It is best to deal with him early."
Mì said:
"Now, with safety and danger still uncertain,
to hastily kill each other—
how would that set an example for those afar!"
Tǐng said:
"When a poisonous snake bites the hand,
a strong man cuts off the wrist,
because what is preserved is greater.
If he gains the upper hand first,
regret will be of no avail."
Mì then followed their advice,
setting up a banquet to summon Rang.
On the Wùwǔ day,
Rang, along with his brother Hóng and his nephew, the Chief of Staff of the Minister over the Masses, Móhóu, went together to see Mì.
Mì sat together with Rang, Hóng, Péi Rénjī, and Hǎo Xiàodé,
while Shàn Xióngxìn and others all stood in attendance.
Fáng Yànzǎo and Zhèng Tǐng moved about inspecting.
Mì said:
"Today we drink with high officials,
we do not need many people."
(High officials,
meaning prominent officials.)
"Only attendants are needed."
Mì's attendants were all dismissed,
but Rang's attendants remained.
Yànzǎo addressed Mì:
"Now we are about to enjoy ourselves,
and the weather is very cold.
For the Minister over the Masses's attendants,
please provide wine and food."
Mì said:
"Let the Minister over the Masses decide."
Rang said:
"Excellent."
Thereupon, Rang's attendants were all led out,
leaving only Mì's strong warrior Cài Jiàndé standing guard with a sword.
Before food was served,
Mì brought out a fine bow
and practiced archery with Rang.
Just as Rang was drawing the bow to full draw,
Jiàndé struck him from behind,
and he fell before the couch,
his cry like an ox's bellow.
Hóng, Móhóu, and Rúxìn were also killed.
Xú Shìjì ran out,
and the gatekeeper struck him, wounding his neck.
Wáng Bódāng shouted from afar to stop him.
Shàn Xióngxìn kowtowed, begging for his life,
and Mì spared him.
The attendants were startled and disturbed,
not knowing what to do.
Mì declared loudly:
"We rose together in righteous arms with you all,
originally to eliminate violence and chaos.
The Minister over the Masses acted tyrannically and cruelly on his own,
insulting and humiliating his colleagues,
with no regard for superiors and subordinates.
Now, only his family has been executed;
none of you are involved."
He ordered Xú Shìjì to be helped and placed under a tent,
personally dressing his wound.
Rang's subordinates were about to disperse,
but Mì sent Shàn Xióngxìn ahead to pacify and console them.
Mì soon rode alone into their camp.
(Rode alone,
meaning rode singly.)
(Ride,
read as qíjì.)
He ordered Shìjì, Xióngxìn, and Bódāng to separately lead the troops,
and both inside and outside, stability was thus restored.
Rang was cruel,
Móhóu suspicious and jealous,
and Rúxìn greedy and unrestrained.
Therefore, on the day they died,
none in their command mourned them.
However, Mì's generals and aides began to harbor doubts in their hearts.
Earlier,
Wáng Shìchōng knew that Rang and Mì would not remain harmonious for long,
hoping they would plot against each other,
so he could take advantage of the situation.
Upon hearing of Rang's death,
he was greatly disappointed,
sighing:
"Lǐ Mì is naturally clear-sighted and decisive;
whether he becomes a dragon or a snake,
truly cannot be predicted!"
On the Rénxū day,
Lǐ Yuān prepared the imperial carriage to welcome the Prince of Dài to ascend the throne as emperor at the Tiānxīng Hall.
(Tiānxīng Hall,
should be Dàxīng Hall.)
A general amnesty was declared and the reign title changed,
changing it to Yìníng.
On the Jiǎzǐ day,
Yuān entered Cháng'ān from the Chánglè Palace.

Yuān was appointed Acting Commander-in-Chief with the Yellow Axe, Commissioner with Extraordinary Powers, Grand Commander of All Military Affairs Inside and Outside, President of the Department of State Affairs, and Grand Counselor-in-Chief,
and further enfeoffed as Prince of Táng.
The Wǔdé Hall was made the Counselor-in-Chief's office,
and his instructions were called orders.
He conducted affairs daily at the Qiánhuà Gate.
(The Qiánhuà Gate,
is located east of the Dàxīng Hall.)
